utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber assumes that the Prosecution wants to respond to the 98 bis submissions made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. We're pleased to have this opportunity to address the Defence motion pursuant to 98 bis. Over the course of today, you will hear from a number of members of the Prosecution, who will address in turn relevant aspects of the motion. I will begin with some preliminary remarks and focus on some aspects of the joint criminal enterprise, the implementation of which will be addressed in greater detail by those who follow. Mr. Russo, for example, will follow me and address the unlawful shelling of civilians. Mr. Hedaraly will turn to the implementation of the common purpose through persecutory killings, burning, looting, detention, and harassment directed at Serbs. Mr. Waespi and Ms. Gustafson will describe General Gotovina's command and control, contributions to the JCE, notice of crimes by HV troops under his command, and failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish. Mr. Margetts will outline General Cermak's role in the JCE and his 7(3) liability. Ms. Mahindaratne will discuss the role played by the special police under the command of General Markac as well as his role in the JCE and 7(3) liability. Now, a few preliminary remarks before I discuss aspects of the JCE, Your Honours, about the legal standard to be applied and a couple of other issues. First, our discussion today will focus on or be in the context of JCE and 7(3), largely because those are the modes of liability primarily focussed on by the Defence. Other modes of liability in the indictment, however, such as ordering or aiding and abetting remain operative and provide a further basis for denial of the 98 bis motion. Nevertheless, in the context of 98 bis, they need not occupy a distinct portion of our presentation in order for the Court to determine that they, too, are supported by the evidence. Your Honours, since the December 2004 amendment, Rule 98 bis does not permit a judgement of acquittal on parts of counts. Therefore, the Gotovina Defence citation to Strugar relies on an anachronistic view of Rule 98 bis which was, as you will be aware, explicitly modified to eliminate the parsing out of counts. If -- first of all, the Trial Chamber may only enter a judgement of acquittal with respect to an entire count of the indictment. That's seen in the recent Prlic 98 bis decision. If a count is comprised of several parts and there is no evidence on one part but there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction on the other parts, the 98 bis motion will fail and that can be seen in Lukic and Lukic. Now, in addition to our observation that the Gotovina Defence erroneously stated the legal standard with respect to counts, we also note that the Defence was wrong in asserting that a sovereign authority is an element of deportation. And I direct the Trial Chamber to both the Stakic Appeals Chamber judgement and the Krajisnik Appeals Chamber judgement. Similarly, contrary to the Defence assertion, the evidence supports the conclusion that a state of armed conflict continued throughout the state of Croatia until the conclusion of a peaceful settlement was achieved in November 1995, and that can be seen at transcripts 4967, line 17, through 4968. Finally, Your Honour, a word on the legal standard for evaluation of 98 bis. A Rule 98 bis decision does not involve the weighing of evidence or an evaluation of the strength or weakness of contradictory or different evidence before the Trial Chamber, and that could be seen in the recent Martic decision. Now, while the Defence has expressly acknowledged aspects of these standards, noting, for example, that the weighing of credibility is not a factor, they have, at the same time, reversed or inverted that standard in some respects, either citing a piece of evidence that purportedly contradicts the Prosecution case as demonstrating that the motion should be granted or urging the Trial Chamber to engage in a weighing of evidence, and find in favour of the Defence. And as I discuss aspects of the JCE I will attempt to identify at least a couple of those examples. Again, the standard is not whether the Defence can cite evidence in support of its theory. The standard, of course, is whether is there any evidence taken at its highest which can support a conviction as to each count. Your Honour, let me therefore turn now to the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove Serbs from the area, to remove them through such means as shelling, destruction, looting, intimidation, and violence. Let me begin by noting what we know about intent related to the JCE. In sum, the Croatian leadership wanted Serbs out, planned to get them out through illegal means, insisted that they weren't coming back, took a variety of steps, including illegal means, to keep them out, boasted about the benefit of having a Serb-free Croatia and, finally, those who saw what was happening on the ground as it was happening recognised that it was intended to get Serb civilians to leave. I'd like to discuss those in somewhat more detail. First -- and I'd like to begin chronologically with the shelling, if I might. First of all, Your Honours, those who were present as the shells rained down and then as they were later lobbed in here and there, those persons who experienced that and observed that, realised that the purpose of such shelling was to panic and drive out the civilian population. And I direct the Court to P926, paragraph 3, Mr. Williams; P931, paragraph 16, Mr. Hendriks; P695, paragraph 30, Mr. Dangerfield. Now that testimony was buttressed by Colonel Konings who, when asked about the firing of projectiles at irregular intervals, recalled his time in Sarajevo and noted that the only purpose of firing artillery at such intervals is to harass a civilian population, to get them to flee, to create chaos, or whatever. That's T14426. Now these conclusions based on contemporaneous experience presuppose an underlying desire to get Serbs out and although these witnesses had no way of knowing that, we now know on the basis of the evidence how right they were. President Tudjman, the leader of Croatia, didn't wanted Serbs in Croatia, and neither did those he surrounded himself with who were likewise convinced, like him, that Croatia was better off without Serbs. Multi-ethnic states, President Tudjman insisted, were unsustainable, unstable, and Serbs, he believed, represented a threat. I'd cite the Court to Galbraith at P444, paragraph 68 and 70, transcript at 4929, and also to P452 of presidential transcript of 29 October 1993. As President Tudjman's Chief of Staff told Ambassador Galbraith, Serbs were a cancer on the stomach of Croatia. That's at P444. And the answer for countries plagued with a multi-ethnic society, according to President Tudjman, was population transfers, about which he spoke openly to Western diplomates such as Galbraith at T4936, or spoke more covertly to other nationalists like Bosnian Serb leadership Koljevic in 1992; that's P459. The intent of the JCE regarding Serbs can also be seen in the barriers erected to prevent their return. As President Tudjman flatly told Ambassador Galbraith, it wouldn't be possible for Serbs to return. "We cannot have these people back." That's at P444, at paragraph 33. And as President Tudjman planned for the return of Croats from South America, he set up laws and barriers to the return of Serbs, "not even 10 percent," P463. Those laws were set up in a way to ensure that Serbs would lose their property when they were unable to get back. See P477. And President Tudjman and Croatian officialdom worked to ensure that the fewest possible number of Serbs would slip through. "If we let 204 persons come here tomorrow you would have 1204, and in ten days 12.000. Nothing for now." P466. So when the political and military situation in late July 1995 caused President Tudjman and others to conclude that the opportunity was ripe for a military solution to the stalemated conflict, President Tudjman met with his key advisors to discuss the operation on the 31st of July. The Defence has suggested to you that the Brioni transcript read in context is "highly ambiguous." Now, apart from the fact that those ambiguities must be resolved against a 98 bis motion, it is also important to note, Your Honours, that the context offered by the Defence referred to the passages purportedly relied upon by the Prosecution but omitted several significant passages. You will hear more about the meeting in Brioni from Mr. Russo shortly, but I'll simply refer to a few key elements that were not mentioned. One, President Tudjman reminded his subordinates of the Croat towns that had been destroyed and that there was now an opportunity to hit Knin with artillery. Two, President Tudjman pointed out that this was not simply an opportunity to have things under control but to give Serbs a taste of what they had given Croats and to pay them back. And, three, it was important that the civilians flee. The army will follow and each will have a psychological effect on the other. Your Honours, the intention to get civilians out was also reflected in the use of leaflets and other forms of psychological operations as you have heard. These further means of getting them out as President Tudjman said, "while pretending to guarantee civil rights, et cetera ... use radio and television but leaflets as well." That's at P461. Minister Susak later bragged to Ambassador Galbraith about using psy-ops to get civilians out. General Gotovina confirmed in his book. General Gotovina confirmed the use of leaflets in his book to get the local population to leave. That's at P113, part 2, page 197. You've seen the purported RSK leaflet with the clear mistake on the stamp that purportedly orders a civilian population to withdraw, that's P480, as well as the MUP report revealing that it was thrown from an aircraft, P484. And you've seen that this process was so successful that it was replicated later, for example, in Operation Southern Move, where a false leaflet purporting to be from the army of Republika Srpska ordered civilians to leave. That's P113, part 2, page 206. Now, with respect to the violence, the killings, the looting, the destruction, burning as with the shelling, Your Honours, there was a contemporaneous recognition by observers on the ground that these events reflected a policy or at least acquiescence, official acquiescence, in those acts. And I would point the Court to P446, US code cable mentioning that the goal was to ethnically cleanse the region of Serbs or P447, referring to systematic looting and burning of Serb property. The Defence has asserted that because there is no explicit reference notice Brioni transcript to use of burning and looting as a means of forcibly removing Serbs or keeping them out that it could not be part of the JCE. There is no basis either in common sense or in the actual backdrop to these events for such a view, Your Honour. Virtually the day before, General Gotovina's forces were burning down Grahovo "in an organised fashion," as Serbs fled to Knin. I would point the Court to P461; P71, the operational diaries between 28 July and 31 July; P1113, part 2, pages 61 through 66; and at transcript at page 16484, lines 8 through 12. As General Gotovina told President Tudjman, he was then going to bring the same troops to Knin, troops who were aching to get there, troops who were hard to keep on a leash. There was no need to specify every means ... every means did not need to be specified for implementing the removal of Serbs and certainly not those particular means. The Defence has also focussed on orders concerning burnings, violence and looting as supporting their 98 bis motion. The Gotovina Defence, for example, has asserted that the Prosecution's position is untenable, because it would be mean that these orders were not meant to be followed and they asserted that they asked Ambassador Galbraith "that particular question." And in essence, I asked -- that is the quote from the Defence: "I asked Ambassador Galbraith did Minister Jarnjak and Minister Susak issue orders that President Tudjman did not want followed?" And the answer was no. Now apart from the fact that this asked the Court to weigh purportedly competing evidence in a manner that has no place in a 98 bis determination, it is in fact a piece of evidence that ignores the witness's position to the contrary, and I'd ask you to what Ambassador Galbraith said about that. He was asked at -- this exchange begins at 5077, 5076 and continues. He was asked: "... were you aware of orders by the minister of the interior or the Ministry of Defence ..." He went on to say he was told of such orders. "I'm sure I was told the Ministry of Interior had given orders." And then the exchange continued: "Mr. Ambassador, if orders were being given to stop criminal activities in the Krajina, then permitting those criminal activities was not state policy, was it?" And that was the thrust of the question, and here are some of the things that Ambassador Galbraith said: "I do not agree with -- with what you've just stated. I have enough experience over the years that I served in Croatia with Croatian officials and Serb officials, giving orders and saying they'd given orders that they had -- and making promises they had no intention of keeping, and I do not believe that the Croatian government made a serious attempt to bring this destruction under control until such time as it was basically -- there was nothing left for the Serbs to return to." And he continues in that vein for nearly a page and he concludes: "My point is, and I believe this, and I -- it comes from very extensive observation of -- on my own part at the reporting of the embassy and lots of other sources that the destruction that took place was something that Croatia could have prevented, chose not to prevent because it served the purposes of the top Croatian leadership." And that is Ambassador Galbraith's answer to whether the orders rendered the Prosecution's position untenable and it is buttressed by such witnesses as Elisabeth Rehn, who testified -- who at P595 stated that she had no doubt that the crimes committed by the Croatian forces were pursuant to orders or silent approval. Just a couple of other examples, Your Honour, of the inversion of the standard that I mentioned earlier. The Defence cited Peter Marti's evidence in support of the position that the destruction was not discriminatory because he said that "sometimes writing down the words 'Croatian house' on a dwelling did not prevent the building from being spared." Now apart from the fact that the use of the word "sometimes" indicates the exception that proves the rule, it overlooks the evidence that dwellings marked as Croatian households were left untouched. Find that at T7915, or another witness T14922 through 23, or the general evidence that it was Serb houses looted while Croatian houses were not. That's P61, paragraph 21. Similarly, the Defence referred to Peter Marti's testimony that his personal opinion was that the looting was not ordered "because you couldn't see any kind of systematic pattern in it, expect from the fact that it was more or less totalled." P415, page 4. Now, apart from the fact that the Chamber would be entitled to infer that more or less total destruction was sufficiently systematic to suggest ordering or at least acquiescing -- acquiescence by the authorities, this evidence also ignores such evidence as P740, report that most buildings were destroyed and systematic looting was taking place; P477, again referring to systematic looting and burning; P807, with the comment: "Beyond any doubt this is a war crime act: The systematic burning of property, houses, stables, haystacks and the like." Or P2151, referring to systematic devastation. There was a reference to the fact that collection centres did not constitute forcible transfer. I would point the Court to the testimony of Ambassador Galbraith at P444, who indicated that he viewed the detention centres as "transition camps" out of Croatia where Serbs were convinced it was in their best interest to leave and that while they were detained, their houses were burned, their livestock killed, in a manner similar to that which he saw after Operation Flash. Paragraph 66. Your Honours, I mentioned it -- I mentioned, Your Honour, earlier that the -- that members of the Croatian political and military leadership led by President Tudjman and including the accused, wanted Serbs out, devised and implemented ways of getting and keeping them out and expressed their satisfaction in a job well done. I didn't address that latter point and would like to conclude by citing the Court to some of that evidence. These are two speeches, one in the relatively immediate aftermath of Storm on August 26th by President Tudjman. I invite the Court to read this in its entirety and get a good feeling from this for the attitude towards Serbs and the intent of the leadership. Let me just read a few lines from this: "This is not just a simple freeing up until now occupied areas. This is creation of foundations for independent and sovereign Croatian state for future centuries. As long as they have been in Knin while Knin was under occupation, future of Croatia hasn't been secure, but after Storm it is. Never again will anybody be able to endanger it." President Tudjman goes on to describe when Knin was captured by Turkish conquerers and "together with them, the ones who stayed till yesterday in our Croatian Knin." But today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm in a continuous attempt to keep your speed at -- at a pace which is still bearable for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would take over part of this task that would be appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Today it is Croatian Knin and never again it will go back to what was before, when they spread cancer which has been destroying Croatian national being in the middle of Croatia and didn't allow Croatian people to be truly alone on its own, that Croatia becomes capable of becoming independent and sovereign state." President Tudjman goes on to discuss the demographics and how there's a high percentage of Serbs in the middle of Croatian land, and he continues: "But to manage that, dear Croatian brothers and sisters, we had to unite." And then an interruption in the recording. And it continues: "All decisions of our leadership the -- have been gone in two, three days, as I have already said. They were gone in a few days as if they had never been here, as I said ... they did not each have time to collect their rotten money and dirty underwear." And then on the one year anniversary of the liberation of Knin, President Tudjman made that point crystal clear. "The results that we have achieved are of historical importance. We have returned Zvonimir`s Croatian town," that's Knin, "to the fold of its motherland, Croatia, as pure as it was in Zvonimir's time." Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to turn the floor over to Mr. Russo, who, as I mentioned earlier, will address issues related to unlawful shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. I will, as you may have guessed address the allegations of unlawful attack. However, I must first address two legal errors in the Gotovina Defence's submission arising from argument that determination of a violation under Article 5 has to be dictated by the laws and customs of war under Article 3. First, they incorrectly argue that the Prosecution is required to prove that the unlawful attack was "widespread and systematic." This is not accurate. First of all, the chapeau elements for persecution are widespread or systematic. In any event, however, for purposes of Count 1, the Prosecution has alleged an unlawful artillery attack as one of many acts of persecution and not as a separate crime under Article 3. As such, the Prosecution need not establish that this sole act was itself either widespread or systematic, and the Court can look to the Kunarac Appeals judgement as well as the Vasiljevic Appeals judgement. Nevertheless, the evidence has indeed shown that the unlawful attack was both widespread and systematic. Second, they incorrectly argue that the Prosecution is required to prove civilian deaths or injury resulting from the unlawful attack. This again misstates the law. The Kordic Appeals judgement, at paragraph 105, specifically states that an unlawful attack against civilians may constitute the crime of persecution without the requirement of a particular result caused by the attack. Nevertheless, again, as I will address further on, the unlawful attack did in fact cause death and injury to civilians. The Gotovina Defence has also incorrectly argued that the unlawful attack is at the core of the Prosecution's case theory against General Gotovina, and that if the unlawful attack allegation fails, then the entire JCE theory fails. As mentioned by Mr. Tieger, the Prosecution has alleged all modes of liability, including aiding and abetting through 7(1), as well as command responsibility under 7(3) for all crimes charged in the indictment. Thus, contrary to the Defence assertions, all crimes charged against General Gotovina are neither dependant on the JCE allegation nor on the allegation of unlawful attack. I will now move to the evidence in the case of unlawful attack. The Gotovina Defence argues that there is no evidence of a single unlawful attack. One can only come to such a conclusion by completely ignoring the testimony of the witnesses who personally observed or were subject to the shelling ordered by General Gotovina, as well as the orders and actions of General Gotovina himself. The evidence shows that General Gotovina ordered an attack on the major population centres of the Krajina and that this attack was directed at the Serb civilian population. Pursuant to General Gotovina's order, purely civilian areas were shelled in the towns of Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac. I'd like to show a demonstrative via Sanction. From this demonstrative, Mr. President, Your Honours, we can see the areas that were shelled according to witnesses Mira Grubor, Andries Dreyer, Joseph Bellerose, Roland Dangerfield, and Eric Widen, all of whom provided evidence that shells landed all over Knin, including in areas nowhere near any alleged military targets. In particular, the north-east side of the town, which is the area around the hospital, as well as the eastern side of the town, are areas where there were no targets for artillery fire in Operation Storm. We know this from the testimony of Marko Rajic, the man who planned and oversaw the artillery attack on Knin, as well as from the evidence of Phil Berikoff and Kosta Novakovic. Let's take a look now at how this pattern of shelling compares with the alleged targets identified by Mr. Rajcic himself. Now what I have done here, Your Honours, is simply reproduce the same areas where the shells landed, and I have highlighted the areas which Mr. Rajcic identified as those which were actually fired upon by Croatian forces, both as pre-planned targets, as well as targets of opportunity. The Court can find this evidence at transcript pages 16369 to 380, 16391 to 398, and Exhibits P2330 up to and including P2335, and P2337. Now, the Prosecution certainly does not agree with Mr. Rajcic that all of the areas he identified were in fact military targets which could be lawfully engaged with artillery. Nevertheless, for purposes of 98 bis, this evidence suffices to demonstrate that contrary to the assertions of Mr. Rajcic, and to those of the Gotovina Defence, the artillery attack on Knin was far from a precise operation aimed only against military targets. Indeed ... indeed, this evidence shows that shells impacted all over the town or, as one could easily find, that the town itself was shelled. The entire town was shelled even despite the fact that there was no military defence of Knin itself, meaning no combat troops, no defence trenches, no anti-tank ditches, no heavy weapon deployments, and no outgoing fire from within the town. Nothing, Your Honours, to indicate that the ARSK had planned to defend Knin from within. This evidence comes from Robert Williams, Roland Dangerfield, and Phil Berikoff. Taken together, this evidence shows that the artillery attack on Knin was not done for the purported purpose of "knocking out" the command and control structure of the ARSK but was in fact directed at the civilian population. There is similar evidence of shells being fired at purely civilian areas of the towns of Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac. In Benkovac, witnesses Dusan Sinobad and Witness 56 testified to the shelling of purely civilian areas. We can see those here. Dusan Sinobad testified there were no military targets in Benkovac proper, with the possible exception of the Macura barracks which was located over a kilometre from the centre of town, though he also testified that there were no ARSK soldiers in that barracks on 4 August. This evidence was corroborated by Witness 56 and by Kosta Novakovic, a member of the ARSK Main Staff, who both testified that there were no combat troops in Benkovac because during Operation Storm they had all been sent to the front-lines. A HV report also demonstrates that the town of Benkovac was indiscriminately shelled. P1200, a report by the 134th Home Guards Regiment states at page 2 that the general area of Benkovac was shelled by the artillery forces of OG Zadar "without monitoring" and that they had received a message from that unit asking, "Is anything falling on Benkovac?" Moving now to Obrovac. In Obrovac, we have -- we have the witness testimony of Jovan Dopudj who testified that areas all over the town were shelled, and based on personal knowledge as a former ARSK commander after that area, that there were no military targets inside the town of Obrovac, which meant no command or communications centres, no combat troops, and no military equipment in the town. That can be found at P548, paragraph 2. Nevertheless, the spread of impacts -- the spread of impacts in the town indicates that shells did, in fact, fall all over the town. Moving now to Gracac. In Gracac, witnesses Mile Sovilj, Vida Gacesa and UNMO Herman Steenbergen, all testified to shells landing in purely residential areas of the town. Also significant to the shelling of Gracac was the testimony from Marko Rajic himself that with the exception of the cross-roads on the edge of town, there were no military targets of sufficient value in Gracac to consider for gaining a military advantage by artillery fire. The Court can find this at transcript page 16 -- transcript page 16 ...

Second, when you talked about Obrovac we saw Gracac on our screen, then it disappeared when you start talking about Gracac. utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But, of course, the memory of a human being is limited in keeping rather complex pictures stored. I'm also addressing the Defence. We know -- we all know that this is just the visualized interpretation of the evidence by the Prosecution. utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I take it that Mr. Kehoe has spoken on behalf of all Defence teams. I see this confirmed. Please proceed, Mr. Russo, in -- at a speed which is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I'm grateful for the agreement. Now, the testimony of Marko Rajic that there were no targets for artillery fire in Gracac with the exception of the cross-roads can be found at transcript page 16365. In addition, Zdravko Janic, the special police commander in charge of the axis of attack which included Gracac, likewise testified that there were no military targets inside the town of Gracac proper. This can be found at transcript 6355 to 356, and 6392. Since the area of Gracac was the responsibility of the special police during Operation Storm, I will return to a bit later in a discussion of Mr. Markac 's contribution to the JCE through unlawful attack. In any case, the shelling of purely civilian areas inside the major population centres of the Krajina is evidence upon which this Trial Chamber could find that the artillery attack was, in fact, directed against the Serbian civilian population. Even beyond this, however, there is yet more evidence to show that the civilian population was the primary object of the artillery attack, because the civilians in the major towns were not the only victims of shelling. Those who lived in the small villages and hamlets around the Krajina where no military presence could be found were also subjected to artillery strikes. You can find this in the evidence of Witness 54. That's at P186, page 5, transcript 2856 to 2857, as well as the evidence of Mr. Jovan Dopudj, that's at 5999 to 6000, as well as P548, paragraph 4, and P551. In addition, the evidence of Sava Mirkovic. That would be at D720, transcript 7418. Evidence that the artillery attack was directed against the civilians does not only come from witnesses and places that were shelled but also from the method and means of attack chosen by General Gotovina. Knin was shelled for 19 hours on the 4th of August, followed by an additional six hours of shelling on the following day with rates of fire varying from intense bombardment at the outset to rounds -- four to five rounds per hour landing during the day and night. This we get from the testimony of Alain Gilbert, Geoff Hill, Robert Williams and Phil Berikoff. The Trial Chamber has seen a video of the artillery attack on 4 August this is P1278, in which the varying rates of fire can be heard. In particular, the single impacts which are unevenly spaced out in time. We know that such sporadic fire was intentional from the orders of General Gotovina at P1125, P2350, and the reports of the TS-4 artillery commander Bruno Milin at P1268. As alluded to a bit earlier by Mr. Tieger, Lieutenant-Colonel Konings testified --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies. Lieutenant-Colonel Konings testified that this type of prolonged shelling with random single rounds would have almost no effect on the military itself, would not deliver any true military advantage, but that it would have a psychologically harassing effect on the civilian population as it would keep them guessing about where the next round would fall. It is in fact this effect on the civilian population, Your Honours, that was truly intended by General Gotovina and the other members of the JCE which is reflected at the meeting which I will come to in a bit. Now, the kind of weaponry used is, of course, another fact which sheds even further light on the true intent of the artillery attack. Mr. Akhavan rightly pointed out that an indiscriminate attack can be found to have been directed against the civilian population. Article 51 of Additional Protocol I defines an indiscriminate attack as "one which employs a method or means of combat the effects of which cannot be limited as required by the protocol and consequently in each such case are of a nature to strike military objectives and civilians or civilian objects without distinction." Now despite the arguments by the Gotovina Defence, the application of Article 51 depends entirely on the circumstances of each particular case, and in the civilian-populated areas in this case, General Gotovina chose to use unguided multi-barrel rocket launcher systems, an unquestionably indiscriminate weapon under the circumstances. This we can find at D1425, paragraph 16, transcript reference is 16278 to 279, 16282 to 285. Marko Rajic himself admitted that using multiple-barrel rocket launchers against targets in a residential area would violate the rules of distinction and proportionality. He made this admission at transcript page 16592. Every other witness who testified about MBRLs, including the special police chief of artillery Josip Turkalj, testified to their extreme inaccuracy and huge area of coverage. We can find this also in the testimony of Andrew Leslie, Harry Konings, and UNMOs, Kari Anttila and Tor Munkelien. Either worse than MBRLS, Your Honours, is the evidence that cluster munitions were used. The evidence that cluster munitions were used against Knin, I refer the Chamber to the evidence of Mr. Murray Dawes, P980, P981, P984, D863, and transcript reference 10500. Finally, the almost complete lack of damage to the alleged military targets in Knin highlights that the civilians were the primary object of the attack. For purposes of economy, Your Honours, I will focus only on some of the "high-value military targets" identified by Marko Rajic. The ARSK HQ. After 25 hours of shelling, the alleged target par excellence, according to Mr. Rajcic, took exactly one shell hit and that shell hit, Your Honours, landed in the parking lot behind the building. This we know from the evidence of Kosta Novakovic, Geoff Hill, and Alain Forand. Indeed, the evidence shows that General Cermak himself moved right into the building after the artillery attack and began using it. The northern barracks, another allegedly high-value target, showed almost no signs of damage and, again, was immediately used by Croatian forces upon their entry into Knin. This we know from the evidence of Murray Dawes, Geoff Hill, Andrew Leslie, and Stig Marker Hansen. The residence of Milan Martic, even though the building in which Mr. Martic lived was targeted and fired upon, Marko Rajcic conceded that the building itself was not a military target but, rather, only Mr. Martic himself. Mr. Rajcic also made clear that he absolutely no information about the building that was targeted and fired upon. He didn't know how many flats were in the building, how many floors it had, how many people may have been living there or who were there on the 4th of August, and he also admitted that the chance of actually injuring or killing Mr. Martic by firing artillery that building was "very slight." The Court can find this at transcript 16446 to 447. Although Mr. Rajcic denied that MBRLs were used when firing at the residence of Milan Martic, UNMO Kari Anttila testified that he conducted a crater analysis of six MBRL impacts in that same residential area and that buildings and cars were damaged. The Court can find this evidence at P60, D166, D167 and D1261. Mr. Rajcic also testified to firing on the "old hospital" building in downtown Knin for the sole reason that he heard Mr. Martic was in there. That's at transcript 16396. Now chasing Mr. Martic around the town with a cannon or a rocket launcher located 25 kilometres away and shooting at any building he might be in, I submit, Your Honours, is a classic example of an indiscriminate and a disproportionate attack. The Gotovina Defence also argues that there was no death and no injury to civilians as a result of the artillery attack ordered by General Gotovina. Even though, as I mentioned, there is no requirement to prove such a result, the evidence does indeed show that between 50 and 75 civilians were killed, and between 30 and 40 were injured during the artillery attack on Knin. This evidence can be found from the testimony of Phil Berikoff, P740, paragraph 2; D284, pages 7 to 9; P747; and P744, as well from the evidence of witness Mila Grubor who was a nurse on duty at hospital on 4 August. That's at P54 and P55, as well as the evidence of Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi, Robert Williams and Exhibit P220. There is also evidence of extensive damage to civilian structures as a result of the artillery attack, despite the arguments to the contrary. In Knin, the UNMO evidence records at least 110 buildings in Knin damaged or destroyed by shelling. That evidence comes from P64 and P67. Mr. Berikoff also testified that he personally observed at least 100 houses in Knin destroyed during the artillery attack and that there was substantial damage to more than these 100 houses which did he not specifically record. That can be found at 7601 to 602, 7882 to 83. Witnesses in Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, also testified that the shelling caused damage to residential and civilian structures in those towns. And I would refer the Chamber to the evidence of Witness 56, Dusan Sinobad, Jovan Dopudj, Vida Gacesa, and Herman Steenbergen. Now, the Gotovina Defence also asserts that there is no evidence that the artillery attack caused civilians to flee. Here again, the evidence on the record proves otherwise. Witnesses for each town that was shelled testified that civilians fled because of the shelling. In Knin, and the smaller villages surrounding it, there is the testimony of Witness 54. In Benkovac and its surrounding villages, there is the testimony of Witnesses 56 and Dusan Sinobad. In Obrovac, there is Jovan Dopudj. In Gracac, testimony of Mile Sovilj and Vida Gacesa. As to any arguments that Mr. Martic's decision to evacuate the women and children was the cause of this mass exodus, I will refer the Trial Chamber to the evidence that Mr. Martic's decision was issued because of the unlawful artillery attack and also the evidence that most civilians were already leaving their towns before Mr. Martic even made that decision, much less communicated it to anyone. And in any event, the evidence shows that they would have left even in the absence of that order. The Court can find this evidence at D923, D928, D929, D930, transcript pages 11968, 11973 to 78. Now all of the foregoing evidence is more than capable, Your Honours, of supporting a finding that General Gotovina conducted unlawful attacks against the civilian population in order to drive them out of the Krajina. Indeed, as it was apparent to those who suffered and who witnessed the artillery attacks, the intent to drive out the Serbian population by unlawful shelling appears plainly from the fact that the towns themselves were shelled. The damage to the alleged military targets is almost nil, in comparison to the damage to the homes and buildings of the civilians who fled for their lives, and to the dead they left behind. This evidence, on top of the evidence of the manner and means by which this attack was perpetrated, provides this Trial Chamber with sufficient evidence to infer that the intent of the attack was to drive the civilians out. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber need not infer what has been plainly expressed. General Gotovina ordered that the major population centres of the Krajina be put under artillery fire and he did so pursuant to the plan reflected at the Brioni meeting. At that meeting, President Tudjman announced that the political climate presented an opportunity to repay the destruction of Croatian towns and villages and he made clear to everyone the importance of getting the Serb civilians to leave so the military would follow. It was General Gotovina who responded to that comment and assured the President that if they kept up the pressure there wouldn't be so many civilians left. We know from the testimony of Marko Rajic that the use of this term "pressure" is a euphemism for the use of artillery. That can be found at transcript 16601. The pressure that General Gotovina was referring to at the Brioni meeting was the artillery attacks which he was conducting at that time against the civilian-populated areas of Cetina and Strmica and which were driving civilians out of those areas and into Knin, spreading panic among the civilian population there. The Court can find this in the evidence of UNMO witnesses Peter Marti and Alexander Tchernetsky, P427, P417, P204 and 205, as well as the evidence of Witness 136, transcript 666 to 67, 797 to 798. In any case, President Tudjman, General Gotovina, General Markac and all who were in attendance at the Brioni meeting were well aware of the effect that artillery had on Serb civilians in the areas they shelled, not only from what they were doing in Cetina and Strmica but also from their recent artillery attacks on Grahovo and Glamoc. President Tudjman reminded everyone how the civilians had fled those towns when General Gotovina's forces "put pressure on them." And we know from Marko Rajic that some of the civilians from those towns fled to Knin. Undoubtedly adding to the panic by the refugees from Strmica and Cetina. President Tudjman assured everyone that even greater panic would break out in Knin once their attack started, and that the excuse of a possible counterattack from Knin would be a good pretext for using artillery against the town. The message, Your Honours, was clear, the plan was explicit. Make them an exit route, shell the towns to trigger the civilian flight and the military will follow them out. That's what exactly what they planned. That's exactly what they did, and that's exactly, Your Honours, what happened. General Gotovina's order to put the civilian-populated towns under artillery fire is a patently illegal order as it explicitly directs his subordinates to disregard the principles of proportionality and distinction and to make entire towns targets for artillery fire. Let me now briefly address General Markac's responsibility for the unlawful artillery attacks against Gracac and Donji Lapac. The special police forces of General Markac were responsible for the axis of attack that included Gracac and Donji Lapac, and General Markac issued the order of attack and engagement of special police rocket and artillery batteries. This can be found at P2385, P614, P552. As I discussed earlier, the shelling of purely civilian areas in Gracac itself is an unlawful attack. There is additional evidence, however, of the indiscriminate nature of the shelling done by the special police forces. The special police chief of artillery, Josip Turkalj, and the commander, Zdravko Janjic, both testified that the special police did not have forward observers. That's at P1150, page 89 to 90; P1151, page 23 to 24; and transcript 13597, as well as P553, page 136. Lieutenant-Colonel Konings testified that artillery should never be used in a civilian-populated area without forward observers. The artillery attack against Donji Lapac, Your Honours is the same story. General Markac ordered the special police forces to capture Donji Lapac and they used artillery to do so. This can be seen from the evidence of General Markac's himself in a report, P585, as well as the evidence of Zdravko Janjic, P552, paragraph 34, D556, page 1, and the evidence of Josip Turkalj, P1151, pages 10, 23, and 32 and transcript page 13611 to 612. There were no military targets and no military presence in Donji Lapac either. Josip Turkalj at transcript 13615, P1151 at page 27. Zdravko Janjic at P552, paragraphs 36 and 37, P553, pages 138 and 150 to 154. Donji Lapac resident Milan Ilic testified that Donji Lapac was shelled for several hours on 7 August 1995, that he left the town because of the shelling, and he could see that houses had been destroyed by shelling as he left the town, as well as the fact that there was no military presence in Donji Lapac. That's at P725, page 1; P726, paragraph 5. Now, the Markac Defence argues in an interesting way that there is no witness who has testified that General Markac had anything to do with the planning and preparing of artillery operations in his axis of attack. This seems to a rather obvious attempt to argue around his presence at the Brioni meeting which reflects the plan to use artillery to get civilians out of the Krajina. The fact that the artillery attacks on Gracac and Donji Lapac follow the same pattern of indiscriminate fire as was carried out by General Gotovina's forces is evidence that General Markac implemented the same common criminal plan. The foregoing evidence, Your Honours, supports a finding that Generals Gotovina and Markac significantly contributed to the common criminal purpose of the JCE by executing the unlawful attacks against Serbian civilians, establishing liability for Counts 1 through 3 of the indictment. In the alternative, the evidence suffices to establish their liability for those same offences through ordering, as well as aiding and abetting under 7(1) and also command responsibility under 7(3). That concludes the unlawful attack presentation. I turn the floor over to Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution has presented a vast amount of evidence regarding what took place in Sector South after the first few days of Operation Storm, as was just described by Mr. Russo. The burning and looting of Serb property, the killing and harassment of Serb civilians and the general untenable conditions of life for those Serbs who remained behind or wished to come back. This evidence included both general and contemporaneous accounts and conclusions from witnesses on the ground, as well as details of specific incidents. Of course, I will not be able today to review all this evidence but will only provide a brief snapshot. I will begin with the destruction. Reports from various international organisations and the testimonies of numerous witnesses are all consistent with respect to the widespread destruction that took place in former Sector South. ECMM reported in late August 1995, at P2151, that 60 to 80 per cent of houses had been partly or completely destroyed. UNMO reported 73 per cent on 13 September, at P97. One member of the UNPROFOR mission, Roland Dangerfield, who travelled 14 hours per day through the area, stated that 80 to 90 of the villages suffered some form of burning. He testified that "the majority of the sector was on fire." This destruction ranged from one end of Sector South to the other, from the municipalities of Drnis to Donji Lapac, Benkovac to Knin, as well as Gracac and Obrovac. In the words of Mr. Vanderostyne regarding the areas he visited, asked to clarify what he meant by burning on a large-scale, he said -- and that has been consistently corroborated by other witnesses, his answer was: "Yes, sure I can. Looting on -- burning on a major scale, those were not isolated incidents. Between Gospic and Gracac the whole countryside was on fire, and I remember, Mr. President, at one time, we were crossing a little -- a small little hill, and you saw the countryside as far as you could look and everywhere, everywhere, every farm, every barn, every annex, every house in the countryside, I mean not in the villages but every single building in the countryside was on fire. So this is what I mean on a major scale." That was at transcript reference 4046, 4047. The destruction started as soon as the HV took control of the territory on 5 August 1995 with Serb houses seen burning in, for example, Zagrovic, Knin municipality; Bukovic, Benkovac municipality; Kakanj in the Kistanje municipality; and Amanovici in the Orlic municipality. The towns of Kistanje, Djeverske, Cetina, Donji Lapac, were more than 95 per cent destroyed. Evidence was presented that this burning occurred after the completion of combat operations. Donji Lapac, which was 99 per cent Serb before the war, was described in the following manner by Minister Susak at a meeting he had with President Tudjman and others: "Donji Lapac, as such, does not exist. There is only its name on the map. Everything is destroyed, everything." That is at P470, pages 53 and 54. In some cases only the church was left intact. Sometimes with soldiers or policemen guarding it. You will hear from that -- on that from Mr. Waespi. The only places spared from such extensive destruction were the larger towns so that they could be repopulated by Croat displaced persons or villages that were populated by Croats in the majority. I refer, for example, to D820, P935, as well as the testimonies of Eric Hendriks at 9747, 48 and 9671, 72; and Stig Marker Hansen, 14933 and 34. The evidence presented by the Prosecution also demonstrated that the widespread and systematic destruction was carried out in numerous cases by Croatian forces. I won't recite all the evidence from witnesses who identified soldiers or people in uniform burning specific dwellings, just a few observations and a few examples. The HV itself noted that its members were committing arson. A report from the political administration coordinator Ivan Zelic on 13 August 1995, that is at D810, states: "It should be noted that the largest number of fires occurred a day or two following the entry of HV units into newly liberated villages. Cases of arson were most often carried out by members of Home Guard regiments who were displaced persons from the areas recently liberated." Looting and burning were also carried out by the special police and there be evidence cited to you by Ms. Mahindaratne later on today. The internationals observed the same thing, P223, an UNCIVPOL report on 20 August states: "Another callous trend in Sector South is the widespread arson of deserted houses in the vicinities of Benkovac, Kistanje, Gracac, and Knin. Croatian military personnel have been spotted at the crime scenes, strongly suggesting that they are the perpetrators. Indeed there is hardly anyone else in the area to blame. The destruction of houses is reportedly accompanied by the looting of property within the extent of this activity indicates that it is officially condoned policy." Two brief examples of the systematic nature of this destruction. In Kistanje, a town I just mentioned as few minutes ago, on 6th August, Mr. Gojanovic testified that he had gone through the town on 6th August and that saw HV soldiers had started to burn it already. Mr. Dawes also observed the town of Kistanje starting to be burned on 6 August. By 9 August it was observed by Mr. Berikoff to be 95 per cent destroyed. As written by journalist Robert Fisk, who was visiting the sector with Alun Roberts, in P684: "Every house in Kistanje has been destroyed by the Croat army: Little bungalows, two-storey villas, Austro-Hungarian buildings of cut stone, the burnt ruins still blessed by trees whose leaves have been autumned browned by the fires. No Serb will ever return here." On the 10th of August in the Kosovo valley, a group of uniformed soldiers was seen going house to house with the support of a fuel truck systematically burning the houses there. That is at P830 and the testimonies of the ECMM witnesses. On the same day, UNMO patrol team observed about 30 to 35 houses burning on the road from Knin to Kosovo. Patrol also observed about the same number of houses burnt down in the area. On the same road at a similar time, witnesses saw anti-aircraft guns used by HV vehicles used to set houses on fire on the road between Knin to Drnis. One of these witness, Switbertus Dijkstra, noted a Puma insignia on the side of one of the military trucks. As noted by a few internationals, it is hard to separate the looting and burning. They usually went hand in hand, with houses looted before being destroyed. The looting was equally systematic and carried out openly. Once again, without going into too much detail, it started as soon as Croatian soldiers entered the area. On 5 August, witnesses Dawes and Williams, among others in the UN compound, saw the Croatian soldiers looting openly, right outside the UN compound. Another witness, Stig Marker Hansen, testified that these looted goods were then collected the next day by a truck and taken away. The looting and burning also continued over time. On 22 August, Mr. Hendriks observed two uniforms military police HV members with a 72nd Battalion insignia, along with three civilians and the support of INA light truck, leaving a house in Guglete in the Obrovac municipality that had just been burned down. There was photograph of that house admitted into evidence. That is at P948. There are also some burning incidents through the months of September, for example, 4 September notice by HRAT at P36, and 10 September by UNCIVPOL at D179. The looting as well spanning the entire area also continued throughout the period of the indictment. For example, reports of 23 and 27 September, noted looting by uniformed personnel in respectively Plavno and Orlic. P2149, P267. The reason internationals were able to observe these acts is that it was done publicly with complete impunity. P933 states units are burning houses while military and civilian police are watching. It is all done in public, and even our presence does not seem to disturb their business. By this fact, the looting must be organised and the burning of houses smells of ethnic cleansing. One report, P1287, noted that in one case, when asked why a professional army was behaving that way, senior HV officer relied: "Why do people drink and drive?" That is at P1287. The effect of all of this, as one international organisation has noted, is that the burning of the Krajina Serb farming resources effectively prevents them to return in larger numbers. Individual small farming constitutes the basic livelihood of Krajina Serbs. That is at P2150. And just to conclude briefly this section, as you heard earlier from Mr. Tieger, the extent of this plunder and particularly the destruction and its systematic nature led to the conclusion by witnesses on the ground that the destruction was either ordered from the top or, at the very least, condoned by the highest authorities. Mr. President, is it a suitable time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Hedaraly. We will have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I would like to go into private session for a second to deal with a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will now move to the charges of murder that were alleged by the Prosecution, and just to inform the Court, based on the Chamber's guidance, the Prosecution will withdraw 32 specific victims that it had identified as victims of murder and subject to Counts 6 and 7. I will not list them now to save time but we will provide the list by e-mail to the parties and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: However, these are the only incidents for which the Prosecution concedes that it has not presented any evidence of murder. As to the other ones, and that is a total of 342, both scheduled and additional killings, evidence was presented that these 342 victims were killed unlawfully. It the Prosecution's submission that the evidence that was presented has to be viewed in its totality. There are various sources of evidence that must be considered in conjunction with each other. There is, of course, evidence from witnesses, both those who have testified live and those whose statements have been admitted under Rules 92 bis and quater, but it is not the only source of evidence. There is not always evidence like that presented by Smiljana Mirkovic or Manda Rodic who eye-witnessed the killing by gun-shot of two different women in cold blood by Croatian soldiers, respectively, Djurdjija Mirkovic in Polaca on 12 August and Jovanka Mizdrak in Mizdrakovac on 8 August. There also is evidence from documents relating to the collection and burial of the bodies, where photographs were often taken by the Croatian authorities in their sanitation operations. There is evidence from international organisations that discovered or otherwise witnessed the bodies on the ground. There are contemporaneous accounts from these organisations about circumstances in which these victims have died. There is evidence from the exhumation and subsequent autopsy and forensic analysis of the bodies. It is therefore an examination of all this evidence in its totality that must be considered, and the Prosecution submits that that evidence in its totality is sufficient for the purposes of Rule 98 bis. We can obviously not today go through all 342 incidents. I will only address a few of the ones specifically raised in the Defence submissions. For example, additional killings number 131 and 132, specifically challenged in the 98 bis submissions of the Gotovina Defence, two unidentified bodies in the hamlet of Dmitrovic in the Zagrovic village. There is no autopsy report for these two bodies, it is true. But there is evidence of unlawful killing. There are reports by both UNCIVPOL and HRAT as well as witness testimony from Mr. Hill who took pictures and testified that they had been shot in the head. Mr. Roberts also provided the Chamber with contemporaneous photographs of the corpses of these two victims and several international and insider witnesses have testified about the problems related to the belated collection of these bodies. I refer to P226, UNCIVPOL report; D3, HRAT report; P292, Mr. Hill's testimony, transcript reference 3770, lines 9 and 10; P303, the photograph. In addition to this evidence, there is a witness, Ilija Mirkovic, who provided evidence that Croatian soldiers entered this hamlet on 5 August, that he heard gun-shots, and that he then discovered the body of another victim on the Prosecution's list, Jovo Dmitrovic, which is victim number 129, and that he had been shot which was confirmed by an autopsy report, which is P1600. So although there is no direct evidence as to how victims 131 and 132 died, there is strong evidence from which to infer that these victims were also shot by Croatian soldiers, the fact that this incident happened in the very same hamlet, around the very same time. But there is also more. In the same village of Zagrovic, which encompasses several hamlets, at least 12 victims on the Prosecution's list of victims died shortly after the end of military operations. In fact, Your Honours heard evidence from Witness 69 regarding one of the scheduled killings in this area. You heard how, on the 5th of August, Croatian soldiers entered the hamlet and the witness heard one soldier take an 80-year-old man behind a house and he heard gun-shots. This victim died of a gun-shot wound to the chest as confirmed in the autopsy report, P1522. You also heard how, in the evening of the 5th of August, the witness found the body of another victim, who had sought refugee at his home, lying in a pool of blood, hours after the Croatian soldiers entered the village. Three other bodies were also found in that hamlet. As I said earlier, we can't do the same exercise today for each of the additional killings. And, of course, we have not submitted for each of them witness testimony, photographs and reports from international organisations, but the point that I'm trying to make, Your Honours, by going in some detail into this incident is that what must be examined is not simply one killing, one autopsy report, for example, but the evidence must be examined in its totality. The same exercise could be made, for example, for the Plavno valley, where there are a number of instances of killings happening in this fashion on the 5th and the 6th of August. Scheduled killing 2, for example, Sava Djuric being pushed in a burning workshop by soldiers comes to mind, and although witnesses have not testified about each and every willing in Plavno at around the same dates, there is strong evidence by this pattern from which to infer that these other killings were similarly unlawful. I know that the scheduled incidents have generally been discussed in court in some detail, so I want to focus on one or maybe two examples, if I have time, of killings for which the Prosecution has submitted witness evidence through Rules 92 bis and/or 92 quater. The first example is found in the testimony of Vesela Damjanic who testified regarding the killing of her epileptic husband, killing 258. As a result of two epileptic attacks, his head -- the head of the victim, Lazo Damjanic, would shake uncontrollably. On the 6th of August, 1995, three young Croatian soldiers entered the village of Vrbnik in camouflage uniforms and the witness testified that they were not from the area. They took the victim towards the road. As they were walking away, the soldiers told him, Just shake your head, will you not do that for very long anymore. As his wife pleaded with the soldiers they told her to get lost or they would kill her. One of the soldiers fired two shots in the air and indicated that the third bullet would be for her. She was hiding behind a tree and waiting. 15 minutes later she heard shooting from the direction where her husband had been taken. Two days later, her husband not having returned and no one giving her any information, the witness saw the very same soldiers who took her husband away, and the soldiers asked her, What are you waiting for, old woman? When told she was waiting for her husband, they told her, You do not have to wait for him anymore, you are not going to see him alive. She responded, If I am not going to see him alive, will I get to see his dead body? The soldiers, If you manage to find him. With the help of her son, the witness eventually found the body of her dead husband under some bushes 15 metres from the road. She testified that when she saw her husband's body, the skull was broken and the stomach was open and that it seems like he had been shot in the stomach many times. In his expert report, Dr. Clark confirmed that there must have been at least six gun-shots. That's P1251, page 12. The body was removed by the Croatian authorities and buried in the Knin cemetery more than two weeks later. No investigation into this killing took place at the time, despite the clear indication of involvement from Croatian soldiers. The only thing she was asked, as we know from her statement, was by one soldier to take a picture of her with her husband's body. When she refused, she was beaten by a man in uniform. When she made a cynical remark about the number of the metal tag assigned to the body, 498, presumably regarding that -- the high number, she was beaten again. I don't have time to go in other examples. I know the Chamber has considered carefully those statements admitted under Rules 92 bis and quater. The Prosecution also refer to those in its submission. At this stage, however, I briefly want to point out that the count for murder in the Prosecution's indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you started so well and now I find that between -- on page 40, between lines 18 and 25, some portions are -- I'm not blaming the interpreters in any way, some parts of the translation in French are missing. Could you please resume where you said -- I'll just read it slowly so that it is on the record: "The only thing she was asked, as we know from her statement, was" -- apparently a request by "a soldier to take a picture of her with her husband's body. When she refused she was beaten by a man in a uniform. And when she made a cynical remark about the number of the metal tag assigned to the body," and then a word is missing, "she was beaten again." Could you please try to -- there was approximately some eight to ten lines which the translation was behind. So would you please re-find your original speed of speech. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. My apologies and thank you for the guidance. At this stage, I briefly want to point out that the count for murder in the Prosecution's indictment is not limited to civilians but also to Serb soldiers who have laid down their arms or are hors de combat. This was not challenged directly in the 98 bis submissions, but we have seen, both during cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses and in written submissions by the Defence, the suggestion that a member of the RSK could not be the victim of murder. This becomes even more relevant considering that all men between 18 and 60 were considered to be ARSK members by the Croatian forces, as stated by Witness 82, P2359, paragraph 28. For example, there has been extensive briefing on the death of Jovica Plavsa, killing 126, in the context of the admission of the statement of his father, Witness 43. And even assuming that the victim was a member of an armed group, which the Prosecution stipulated to, given the contradictory evidence on this point, the more important point is that the victim was taken in handcuffs by Croatian soldiers on 5 August, and after ten minutes or, so the father heard a single shot, and then found his son's body. The autopsy report confirmed that Jovo Plavsa had been buried in handcuffs and that he died of a gun-shot wound to the head and chest, P1597. Even if he was an ARSK soldier, he was in the custody, in fact in handcuffs, of the Croatian soldiers and his killing, the Prosecution submits, was therefore unlawful. Similarly, you heard from witness Marija Vecerina about how her son and four other young Serb men were taken out of a basement by Croatian soldiers, and after hearing some shots, never seen again. This was corroborated by the statement of Zdravko Buncic, admitted under Rule 92 bis. The autopsy reports for these five men were that four died of gun-shot injuries to the head and that the fifth of a gun-shot injury to the neck. Finally, the last aspect of the murder I want to examine is the challenge by the Gotovina Defence in its Rule 98 bis submissions regarding number of incidents that had claimed the autopsy -- where it claimed the autopsy report could not conclude with certainty of a specific cause of death. As an initial matter, the Prosecution notes that for killings number 218, 220, and 288, there is in fact a determined cause of death in the autopsy reports, and they are not unascertained. P1641, P1257, and P1683. In any event, the mere fact that an autopsy may not be able to provide a certain cause of death is not in itself inconsistent with a finding that a victim was unlawfully killed. For example, a number of people we have seen the body before it was collected and clearly stated that he had been shot, like we've seen earlier in the case of additional killings 131 and 132. In some other cases, even where the autopsy could not conclude the cause of death with precision, there can nevertheless be evidence in the report itself that the death was not from a natural cause. So one brief example on this score, additional killing 193, where the autopsy report, P163, says unascertained. That is only because "a fragment of the skull was present, therefore a high velocity gun-shot injury or blunt head injuries cannot be excluded. In other words, there was no head." It is the Prosecution's submission that people don't lose their head from natural causes and that therefore there is strong circumstantial evidence of an unlawful killing. There is more. According to the death report, the death occurred in Golubic near Knin on 11 August. Victim 124, a different victim not specifically channelled by the Defence, was also found in Golubic and killed a few days earlier. His head was found 50 metres away from his body. The autopsy report, P1596, confirms that the head of the victim was not buried with the rest of the remains. The HRAT daily report, P27, indicates that members of the 4th Brigade were involved in the initial operation and remained in the area of Golubic until about 12 August. There also evidence in the Croatian Helsinki Committee report, P2345, page 150, footnote 19, that soldiers were playing football with the head. Just a quick word on Counts 8 and 9, the Prosecution has provided evidence with respect to these counts. I simply refer the Court to the testimony of Draginja Urukalo, who testified via videolink about being forced to strip to her underwear and ordered to play basketball behind her house by Croatian soldiers, even if she was in her 70s at the time. The Prosecution also refers to the evidence of Bogdan Brkic, who provided a statement that he was tied to a tree by Croatian soldiers and a fire was lit under his feet. These are only a few examples, Your Honours. There were countless incidents of threats, beatings and harassment of the Serbs that remained in the Krajina reported by various organisations. Some Serbs were asked why they had not left. For example, P950, a man armed and in uniform told a Serb civilian: "Chetnik go away, this is not your country." You also heard of evidence of Witness 136 who testified being harassed by HV members when she left the UN camp and asked why she did not leave. She also testified about HV firing over the UN camp and scaring the Serbs who had sought refuge there. Mr. Russo discussed the massive departure of the Serb civilians because of the unlawful artillery attack of the 4th and 5th of August. A number of the small Serb population left behind also left following these actions I have discussed today. The looting, the burning, the killing the harassment, the intimidation; in short, the hostile environment created for the remaining Serbs in the Krajina. As late as 27 September, ECMM reported regarding residents in Plavno: "Most people are getting more and more desperate due to the ongoing looting and harassment. They want to leave immediately to Serbia." P2147. The Chamber may also recall the testimony of Witness 13 who was injured by Croatian soldiers and sought refugee at the UN camp. When asked in court why after seven weeks she decided to go to Belgrade rather than go back to her home, she responded: "How could we possibly go back home if our home had been burned down. We had no home to go back to." Witness 1, who was seriously wounded in the same incident, stated that because of the shooting the first few days, he was afraid someone might kill him if he went back to his home. He therefore also left to Serbia. When asked if he would have gone home absent those concerns, he said, Well, yes I didn't have any other country. I was born in Croatia and that was my country. Finally, Witness 69, who I mentioned earlier in his connection with one of the scheduled killing incidents, when discussing the fact that he had stayed behind while others in his hamlet had left on 4th of August and asked him to go with him, when he was asked who asked him to go with them to leave on the 4th he said, Well, neighbours, they tried to convince me that I should go and so did my wife. But I said why should I go? Where should I go? Why would I leave my home? Why would I leave my house? But at one point the time came were I really had to go. I had to leave it. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will turn the floor over to Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will cover aspects of General Gotovina's criminal responsibility under Articles 7(1) and 7(3). First of all, I would like to describe his effective control, and then move on to his shared intent and contribution to the JCE as outlined by Mr. Tieger. Your Honours, there is no doubt that General Gotovina had both de facto and de jure command and control over all forces subordinated or attached to the Split Military District during Operation Storm and throughout the indictment period. Rajcic testimony at 16560 to 62. There is evidence that General Gotovina was a forceful and effective commander capable not only of issuing orders but making sure that his orders were implemented on the ground. You will recall the evidence of Mr. Rajcic that it was very dangerous not to comply with an order from General Gotovina, page 16454. There is evidence that General Gotovina's orders were indeed implemented by the troops on the ground. See Liborius, at page 8273, and P845. The images captured of General Gotovina during 6 August meeting in Knin, D792, demonstrate a confident military commander in full possession of the authority to not only voice his displeasure at what he deemed to be an unacceptable state of affairs created by subordinates, but also to issue direct orders to rectify that situation and to have them implemented. Unfortunately, his focus during that meeting was on supplying crosses, cleanliness and state propaganda for an impending visit of President Tudjman. There is ample evidence, Your Honours, in relation to the 72nd Military Police Battalion that it was part of the Split Military District. The evidence shows that General Gotovina had the material ability to order the military police to take measures to prevent, investigate and punish crimes. P880, in particular Articles 8, 9, 16, 25. Damir Simic, who was a member of the crime police section of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, confirmed that: "Although formally the MP belonged to the head of the MP administration in Zagreb, in their daily activity the MP command would get orders from the Military District Command," and daily activity included maintenance of discipline, investigation of crime, securing check-points, and so on. P967 at paragraph 16. General Lausic confirmed that Article 10 of these Rules fall within the regular military police tasks, and therefore, under Article 9, while performing these regular military police tasks, MPs were subordinated to the commander of the Military District. Contrary to the Defence assertions, there is ample evidence that General Gotovina and his subordinated unit commanders use their subordinated MP units on numerous occasions for non-combat related tasks. Just a few examples. The first one is P1126, plan of security measures, issued by the command of OG North, specifically approved by General Gotovina. Here the military police are ordered "collecting and transporting the population trapped in liberated areas to collection centres. Further, they have to discover and arrest enemy soldiers and prevent incursions of civilians into liberated territory." Page 4. Another example of the non-combat related use of military police is D773, a very detailed order that you might recall, Knin 95, dated 23rd August, in which General Gotovina gives very specific tasks to various units of the district, including military police, in relation to guaranteeing the security of the president. It is telling that General Gotovina was able to issue orders to his subordinates, including the military police, to successfully secure the presence of Croatia in a war-torn area that only a few weeks prior had been enemy territory. Couple of other examples of the non-combat related use of MP, P1113, at page 370, an order by General Gotovina to the MP battalion to prevent torching, or P1123, an order again by General Gotovina to the MPs to set up check-points. Your Honours, there is further evidence - and I won't go into details - that the HV forces operating within the Split Military District were part of a disciplined army and had a functioning chain of command where orders were followed. Marko Rajic, page 16328. Ambassador Galbraith said that the HV was the most disciplined military and best military in the former Yugoslavia. Page 4947 ... As would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, it is easier for me to follow your argument directly rather than to have -- constantly having to check with the French translation or, of course, I can't check the other translation, that then I'm listening French, reading English, which confuses me. So to the extent the Prosecution could develop a similar system as I sometimes saw the Defence doing, that is that one of your people would check carefully how much you are behind that would -- I would really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, Mr. Saklaine has that role already. I just didn't obey him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Another example are the inspections that were carried out if deficiency occurred in units, example P27197, inspection of the 72nd Military Police ordered by General Gotovina. P1132, that is acknowledgment by General Gotovina himself that command and control of units was uninterrupted at the required level during Operation Storm. Your Honours, there is evidence that General Gotovina and his units maintained a strong presence in the Split Military District well beyond 9 August 1995. There is also evidence that General Gotovina spent a significant amount of time in and around Knin during the relevant period of time. Examples P543, a report dated 12 August, of which General Gotovina was appraised of what is happening in the ground. Other examples, P895, document of 20 September, documenting General Gotovina's presence in Knin and his familiarity with the situation on the ground. The interview with General Cermak at page 23, interview of 2004, saying that Mr. Gotovina would come and go. He left for Bosnia but he came back and there are further notes in General Cermak's interview. Other examples, P1131, P1143, and P1013, all documenting the presence of HV units and General Gotovina in the Knin area beyond 9 August. In terms of General Gotovina's ability to prevent or protect property from being destroyed, there is evidence that General Gotovina selectively used his authority issue such orders and control his troops. Mr. Hedaraly already mentioned a couple of incidents about the devastation of Serbian homes and that the Orthodox churches were spared. See, for instance, P807. In the face of the widespread devastation throughout the area and the relative hands-off approach to churches, many of the international observers concluded that there was a policy not to destroy the churches. P988, Marker Hansen. And that General Gotovina must have issued an order that they be protected. There is evidence that guards were posted at some religious locations on the orders of General Gotovina. Comes from Liborius. The fact that most of the churches remained untouched demonstrates that General Gotovina was able to exercise his authority over his troops and ensure that orders were implemented. However, he chose to be selective. You will hear, Mr. President, that -- from Ms. Gustafson that General Gotovina had notice that crimes were being committed by his subordinates during and after Operation Storm, and that he did issue orders in relation to prevention of looting and burning.
