Despite both the notice and orders to prevent, HV members continued burning and looting. General Gotovina had further notice of crimes and his response was to issue another order, that HV members should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is it not only the French translators which have problems, Mr. Waespi, but the B/C/S translation is also behind. I can't listen to two channels at the same time. But could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. General Gotovina's response was to issue another order that HV members should not burn and loot, and again, despite that order, the looting and burning continued. This was a cycle that repeated itself. The non-compliance with General Gotovina's repeated orders to stopped should not be seen as evidence of his lack of effective control over his troops. Quite the contrary was demonstrated through his ability to protect the churches and the President. Your Honours, there is evidence moving to the JCE part that General Gotovina shared the common criminal purpose outlined by Mr. Tieger. Won't go into details again as it relates to the artillery attack, but mention a couple of additional points. A review of the Brioni meeting transcript make it clear that General Gotovina was actively engaged in the planning of the operation and receptive to the suggestions and objectives of his superiors. General Gotovina followed through on the plan discussed at Brioni, as demonstrated by subsequent comments, actions and omissions. In terms of General Gotovina's attitude towards reports that crimes were committed by his subordinates, there is evidence that when faced with such allegations, General Gotovina impliedly condoned and justified these acts. Just two examples, P895, when General Gotovina expressed the attitude being put on notice of crimes by his subordinates that: "He regards it as a human feeling to hate an enemy who has burned, looted and expelled one's family." Similarly, P2499, showing the condoning attitude of General Gotovina. I will conclude by General Gotovina's contribution to the JCE in addition to what Mr. Russo, Mr. Tieger already mentioned. Already General Gotovina's overall plan of attack of 2nd August included, and that's P1126, that civilians were to be transported into collection camps. This demonstrates General Gotovina's intent to get the population out of their homes, rather than to protect their property. And you recall Ambassador Galbraith's testimony that he saw the detention centres as transition camps out of Croatia. P446; and P444, at paragraph 66. There is also relevant JCE evidence in General Gotovina's participation in the sanitation system. P496 is General Gotovina's order of 11 August 1995 to establish a sanitation team to collect human bodies which can be viewed as an effort to collect and bury murder victims without investigating their cause of death. Support provided on this point by Witness 86, P487. Finally, Mr. President, Your Honours, a key contribution of General Gotovina to the JCE was his inactivity vis-a-vis the crimes that were committed by his subordinates against the Serbs and their property. By failing to take genuine measures to prevent, investigate or punish these crimes, General Gotovina effectively condoned and encouraged the commission of further crimes against Serbs. He and his subordinate commanders were primarily responsible for the climate of impunity described by internationals, P451. Maintaining military discipline is first and foremost the task of the commander, not the MP. Theunens, 13309; and Lausic, P2159 at paragraph 210. General Gotovina was the commander of Operation Storm capable of devising a plan, issuing orders and leading men into battle to swiftly achieve the objectives set out by his superiors. Apart from issuing a few generic and hollow orders, General Gotovina chose to take no steps to enforce those orders, while at the same time being aware that such a failure would result in the commission of further crimes. It is within this climate of impunity that Serbs and their property were systematically targeted and victimised by those under the command of General Gotovina. The result was an unbearable and hostile environment in the Krajina which left those few Serbs that remained after the shelling with little choice but to leave their home. In that context, Your Honours, the inference can be drawn that the soldiers under the command of General Gotovina had been given free reign to loot and burn and even kill with impunity in furtherance of the objective of forcibly removing the Serbian population from the Krajina. And there is a concluding remark, observation by Ambassador Galbraith, P44 at paragraph 46: "These were serious and systematic crimes for which the Croatian leadership is fully responsible. Given the disciplined nature of the army and that the leadership was fully in command and had full power to prevent, these were crimes committed on orders or it was a matter of state policy to tolerate or encourage them." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson. I take it that you will be seconded in a similar way by your colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to keep your speed of speech under control. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi has addressed General Gotovina's effective control over the forces subordinated or attached to the Split Military District during the indictment period, and Mr. Hedaraly has described some of the evidence showing that General Gotovina's subordinates carried out the crimes charged in the indictment. I will be addressing the evidence that supports the conclusion that General Gotovina had either actual or inquiry notice of the commission of these crimes and that he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish them. Mr. Russo has covered these elements in relation to the crimes underlying the artillery campaign, and therefore I won't be addressing this evidence. A commander's duty to prevent or punish crimes is triggered when he either knows or has reason to know that crimes are about to be committed or have been committed by his subordinates. As the Appeals Chamber held in the Strugar case, a commander has reason to know that crimes are about to be committed or have been committed by his subordinates where he has "information of a nature, which at the least, would put him on notice of the risk of offences by indicating the need for additional investigation in order to ascertain whether such crimes were committed or were about to be committed." That's at paragraphs 297 to 302. In addressing the evidence of General Gotovina's notice of the charged crimes, I will focus on the crime of murder as this has been specifically challenged by the Defence. The Defence position is that General Gotovina did not know or have reason to know that his subordinates were committing murder because his awareness of the disposal of bodies by sanitation crews does not establish either that the deaths were unlawful or that his subordinates were responsible. That was at page 17279. This assertion is flawed in two respects. First, it reflects a misapprehension of the relevant legal standard, which is not whether General Gotovina received information establishing that his subordinates had committed murder but whether he had information notifying him of a risk of such offences. Second, General Gotovina's knowledge that sanitation crews were collecting and disposing of bodies during the indictment period is just one of the many factors that, when taken together, put him on notice of the risk that his subordinates had committed or might commit murder. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that at the time General Gotovina ordered the attack on the Krajina, he had information that put him on notice of a risk that his subordinates might commit crimes against Serb civilians and their property. Furthermore, this evidence together with the evidence showing his participation in a joint criminal enterprise is sufficient to conclude that he participated in that JCE, knowing that murder and cruel treatment, as well as plunder, wanton destruction and persecution, were at least possible consequences of its execution and he willingly took that risk. First, General Gotovina knew of the widespread commission of crimes, particularly burning and looting, immediately prior to the operation by the same units he used to carry out Operation Storm. And this is clear from the numerous references in the Split Military District operational diary to the looting, burning and destruction by HV members in Grahovo and Glamoc during Operation Ljeto. In addition, General Gotovina was well aware of the sense of bitterness that prevailed after four years of a brutal ethnic war between Serbs and Croats, and he knew that his subordinates, particularly the Home Guard Regiments, were motivated by revenge, as he explained to President Tudjman in Brioni. General Gotovina also knew that this revenge element among his subordinates increased the risk that they would commit crimes against the Krajina Serbs and their property, because he referred to this same desire for revenge to justify their crimes when he was confronted with them. See Exhibits P383 and P895. Before Operation Storm, General Gotovina also correctly predicted that some Serb civilians would remain in the Krajina following the artillery attack and those who did remain would be among the most vulnerable. Namely, those who have to stay, who have no possibility of leaving, P461. And finally, on the 4th of August, General Gotovina ordered his subordinates to shell or at least was aware that they were shelling the Serb civilian population through an indiscriminate artillery attack. The knowledge that his subordinates were firing on civilians must have signalled to General Gotovina the risk that once his ground forces entered the territory they, too, would violently target those Serbs who had been unable or unwilling to flee. This evidence is sufficient to conclude that at least by the 4th of August, General Gotovina had information that put him on notice of the risk that his subordinates may commit each of the crimes charged in the indictment, thereby triggering his duty to prevent those crimes. Immediately following the launch of Operation Storm, those risks became reality. As Mr. Hedaraly has described, on the 5th of August, Croatian ground forces began killing and mistreating the Serbs who remained in the area, and looting and burning their homes. At least by the 6th of August, General Gotovina had actual knowledge of these crimes. At the meeting in Knin that morning he described his subordinates as "barbarians and vandals who are paid with war booty and wage war for war booty." At this time General Gotovina would also have seen the smoke rising from the villages around Knin, as described by Dzolic when he went to the Knin fortress on the morning of the 6th of August; P875 and P876. General Gotovina would also have heard the explosions and the small-arms fire coming from downtown Knin and he would have seen the fires in Knin itself as reported in P106, P825, and P826. And he would likely have seen or received reports of some of the dozens of dead civilians showing signs of deliberate killings by small-arms fire that were scattered along the roads around Knin, such as those witnessed by Murray Dawes and Andries Dreyer. Having witnessed for himself the burning and looting and signs of killing around Knin, the next day, General Gotovina received a report from his own political affairs department that his subordinates were behaving similarly in the zone of operations of OG Zadar, and particularly Benkovac. That's at P1113, part II, page 326. By the 8th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: By the 8th of August the situation was such that General Forand expressed his concerns about the risks to the civilian population and warned General Gotovina of them. P347. Those risks are also apparent in a 10th of August report from the SIS commander for OG North to the Split Military District Command, P1134. It states that in Knin "some HV members drove and seized cars about the town, under the influence of alcohol, making noise, shooting, and threatening people's lives." The next day, the 11th of August, General Gotovina established a sanitation detachment under his command. P496. Consistent with the procedure implemented by the civil protection department, the order makes no mention of conducting criminal investigations. The following day, the 12th of August, General Gotovina receives confirmation that his subordinates are burning and destroying property, slaughtering livestock, and mistreating civilians and prisoners of war; and that is through Exhibit P918. And throughout the remainder of August and September, he continues to receive information from a variety of sources that add to his actual or inquiry notice that his subordinates were murdering Serb civilians, in addition to burning, looting and the slaughter of livestock. For example, contemporaneous media reports of crimes included reports of murders in the area. P2319; P686; P712; P687; P451, page 243; and P685 are examples. And General Gotovina monitored such media reports of HV crimes. This is clear from his 5th of September meeting with General Forand, at which he threatened to execute the UN press officer, Alun Roberts. In his subsequent letter to General Cervenko explaining his actions, he cited a statement made to journalists by Mr. Roberts, reporting that the Croatian army is burning, looting and violating human rights. P383, P385 and P407. The signs indicating that Serb civilians were being murdered by HV members were readily apparent to those monitoring and observing the situation and must have been apparent as well to General Gotovina who was well acquainted with the situation on the ground through various means including the SIS, PD and his unit commanders. The evidence of Mr. Rajcic, P918, and page 28 of General Cermak's 2004 suspect interview confirm this. Numerous witnesses described the signs on the ground indicating the murder of Serbs by HV members. For example, Mr. Morneau testified that under the circumstances it was just a matter of deduction that some of the bodies found on the streets had been murdered by the military. Page 4006 to 4007. Similarly, Witness 84 gave evidence that: "Most of the bodies were said to be victims of war, which was a way of trying to cover up ... when people were killed after Storm, it was obvious that these killings had nothing to do with the operation itself." P1036. If these signs weren't enough, on the 16th of September, General Gotovina received direct notice from General Lausic that the MP had not been able to "completely prevent the commission of crimes, especially theft of property, torching houses, and individual acts of murder." D567. At the same time, reports from the sanitation teams indicate General Gotovina's knowledge that large numbers of corpses are being collected and buried. See, for example, P507, a report from General Gotovina's sanitation detachment to the Main Staff, indicating that 418 corpses had been "cleared up in the Split Military District." In summary, Your Honours, the evidence is sufficient for the Chamber to conclude that within the first few days of the operation, General Gotovina possessed information that indicated at least the risk that his subordinates had committed the crimes charged in the indictment that triggered his duty to punish those crimes. The same information notified him of the risk that his subordinates would continue to commit those crimes, triggering his duty to prevent them. The evidence further supports the conclusion that with this notice General Gotovina failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish the crimes of his subordinates. This inquiry, whether a superior has fulfilled his duty to take necessary and reasonable measures, is a matter of evidence to be assessed on a case-by-case basis. The Defence reliance on other cases to determine what is necessary and reasonable in the context of this case is of little assistance. In this case the evidence supports the conclusion that, prior to the commencement of Operation Storm, General Gotovina failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of the charged crimes. As the Defence has pointed out, the attack order and the relevant attachments, P1125, P1126 and D201, contain generic instructions to "prevent burning and looting." However, in light of the clear risk that General Gotovina's subordinates would commit these and other crimes, the instructions do not constitute necessary and reasonable measures. First, General Gotovina knew that his subordinates had looted and burned Grahovo and Glamoc immediately before Operation Storm. He failed to punish the perpetrators of those crimes and he used the same subordinates to carry out Operation Storm. See P71; P1113, pages 61 to 66, and page 310, the evidence of Dzolic. As the Strugar Appeals Chamber noted "a superior's failure to punish a crime of which he has actual knowledge is likely to be understood at least as acceptance, if not encouragement, of such conduct, with the effect of increasing the risk of new crimes being committed." Secondly, similar orders to those contained in the attack order had already been proven to be ineffective. The 29th of July operational diary records General Ademi stating that "setting of fire to houses is forbidden." Yet the next day, the military police reported that members of the 4th Guards Brigade, 7th Guards Brigade, 114th Brigade, and 126th Home Guard Regiment entered Grahovo and "began setting fire to houses in an organised fashion." P1113, page 66. These two factors alone would be sufficient to conclude that General Gotovina's mere repetition of earlier failed orders did not constitute necessary and reasonable measures. In addition, the attack order contains no instructions to unit commanders relating to the punishment of crimes that, at this point, are a virtual certainty, measures such as engaging the military police, conducting investigations, imposing disciplinary measures, or initiating criminal proceedings. Among the many tasks directed at the military police in these documents, the only one relating to the investigation or punishment of crime is the order to discover, arrest, and bring in enemy soldiers and officers. Crucially, the attack order contains no measures to ensure the implementation of the order to prevent burning and looting, such as instructions to monitor or report on its implementation. And in spite of the risks to the safety of the Serb civilian population in the circumstances of this attack, there are virtually no measures aimed at protecting them or preventing crimes against them. Just a generic instruction to political affairs officers to "advise members of units on conduct with civilians and POWs, in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." D201. The Defence have also pointed to the orders that General Gotovina issued after the commencement of Operation Storm which on their face suggest an attempt to prevent the continued commissions of crimes. In particular, on the 6th of August, D792; the 10th of August, D204; and the 16th of August, P71, page 107 and 108. Yet the evidence supports the conclusion that none of these orders, either individually or cumulatively, constituted necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the wave of crime against Serbs and their property carried out by General Gotovina's subordinates. Two factors stand out in particular. First, the orders relate almost exclusively to the prevention of burning and looting. They contain little, if any, reference to crimes of mistreatment and killing of Serbs despite the fact that General Gotovina had information mounted over time that notified him of the risk that his subordinates might be committing such crimes. And second, although there are slight variations in their wording, these orders more or less repeat the generic instruction to prevent burning and looting. Other than the cynical threat issued to units burning down houses that they will have to spend the winter in them, recorded in the operational diary, General Gotovina took no measures aimed at securing the implementation of these orders which he knew were not being followed. As Mr. Theunens explained, "Things will not get better just by reissuing orders." A commander must take steps to ascertain why his order has not been followed and then take additional measure in order to guarantee his orders are implemented. The Chamber has received evidence indicating the kinds of measures General Gotovina could have - and failed - to take. These measures are apparent from the orders he issued in relation to other matters. I refer the Court to P1142, D655, P1018 and 1019, P1033, and D773. It is the position of the Gotovina Defence that General Gotovina set his command climate at the 6th of August videotaped meeting. That's at page 17269. The Prosecution agrees. At this meeting, knowing that his subordinates are committing crimes and that his instructions to prevent burning and looting have not been followed, General Gotovina takes steps to clean up the town in anticipation of the President's visit. He issues no orders to identify or punish his subordinates who have committed crimes, no orders to stop the ongoing crime or prevent further crimes, and no measures to ensure the implementation of his prior failed orders. The evidence, Your Honours, supports the conclusion that General Gotovina had no genuine intent to implement his orders to prevent the charged crimes and that he repeatedly and persistently failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to stop their commission. This evidence is not only sufficient to ground his superior responsibility, it also supports the conclusion that General Gotovina condoned, assisted and encouraged their commission thereby significantly contributing to the JCE and aiding and abetting the commission of crimes by his subordinates. There is also sufficient evidence to conclude that General Gotovina failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish his subordinates for the crimes charged in the indictment. First, none of his orders to prevent crimes include any instruction to investigate the crimes that he knew had happened. Secondly, although it is the position of the Gotovina Defence that General Gotovina did not have the authority to order the military police to investigate or punish crimes, as Mr. Waespi explained, the evidence supports the contrary conclusion. Namely, that he had this authority and he chose not to exercise it in relation to crimes against Serbs and their property. And the evidence shows that General Gotovina failed to use the disciplinary system that was at his disposal to punish his subordinates' crimes. His orders to prevent burning and looting did not direct his subordinate commanders to impose disciplinary measures in relation to these crimes, and this can be contrasted with examples in P1034, and P1028, and P1013, in which he ordered his subordinates to impose disciplinary measures in relation to other matters. Mr. Theunens concluded that General Gotovina had a narrow interpretation of the concept of military discipline, exclusively focussed on the accomplishment of combat tasks and combat operations. Page 12868. Mr. Lausic echoed this view at P1259, and General Gotovina himself confirmed his narrow approach to military discipline when, on the 15th of August, in the midst of an HV crime wave he reported to the Main Staff that military discipline and combat morale was exceptionally high in the preparation, course and conclusion of combat operations. P1132. Contrary to the assertion of the Defence, the evidence indicating that General Gotovina demobilised soldier who is committed charged crimes did not constitute a necessary and reasonable measure to punish them. Ljiljan Botteri confirmed that there was no systematic reporting of these demobilisations to the Military District Command. She was not aware of any effort to obtain information on how many soldiers were being demobilised for misconduct or the nature of such misconduct, and she was unable to identify any specific case where criminal proceedings were initiated against such a demobilised soldier. The evidence supports the conclusion that this practice was a reckless measure that General Gotovina used in an attempt to transfer responsibility for the criminal elements among his subordinates to another authority. The necessary and reasonable measure in the circumstances would have been to keep the perpetrators within the military structure, and ensure their adequate punishment through disciplinary and/or criminal measures. In conclusion, Your Honours, the evidence adduced by the Prosecution is sufficient to support a finding that General Gotovina knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit or had committed crimes in relation to all counts in the indictment and he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Hedaraly, would this be a suitable time to have a break first and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. If we take a 20-minute break, we should be able to finish by today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, I will address the submissions made by the Defence for Ivan Cermak. The first issue I'd like to address is the issue of effective control. Mr. Kay, in his oral submission and his further note, set out a number of indicators of effective control. Whether any particular accused possesses effective control is determined on a case-by-case basis, taking into account all relevant indicators. Some relevant indicators of effective control that the Defence did not mention include the following. First, the procedure used for appointment of an accused (See Halilovic trial judgement, paragraph 58). The Court will recall that General Cermak was appointed by the supreme commander, Franjo Tudjman. Exhibit D31. Second, the position within the military or political structure. Boskoski trial judgement, paragraph 411. The Court will recall that General Cermak received direct ordered and provided reports directly to the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, D561, P1219. General Cermak was also in direct contact with Franjo Tudjman and the minister of the interior, Ivan Jarnjak. Now, General Cermak refers to that in his 1998 interview, we don't have exhibit numbers for the interviews that have been admitted, so I will just refer to the interviews by their dates. Third, the authority to apply disciplinary measures, Strugar trial judgement paragraphs 393 to 397. He was vested with the authority to ensure order and discipline; Article 52 of Exhibit D32. Fourth, in general terms, it is the reality of the authority of the accused that is at issue. Kordic trial judgement from 2001, paragraph 418. In addition to the matters referred to above, General Cermak held a high rank in the military, and he was a former assistant defence minister, former minister for the economy, and advisor to the President. That's his 1998 interview. He was known and trusted by the President and supreme commander, Franjo Tudjman. 2001 interview. Throughout this case, and during the course of the Defence submissions, the Defence have sought to lessen the impact of the evidence of the international witnesses. The international witnesses who were present, meeting with General Cermak daily as they did their best to carry out their humanitarian missions. The Defence argue that their evidence is limited since they could not see the workings of the Croatian state from the inside, regardless of the extent to which these inner workings were manifest in the external expression of the state organs and actors. However, the Defence failed to mention that not only the international witnesses, but insider witnesses, too, provided consistent and corroborative assessments of General Cermak's authority. The insider witness, Stjepan Buhin, a high-level member of the MUP in Zagreb deployed as a coordinator in the Kotar-Knin region, a witness who was centrally placed in the state structures and could observe the functioning of the state from the inside, described General Cermak's authority as follows. He stated that: "Cermak was the commander in chief in Knin." "He was the main commander of the army." He stated: "General Cermak was the highest ranking officer that we worked with, in terms of coordinating the army," and "no one outranked him in the area." In regard to the area of General Cermak's authority, Buhin stated that his area of responsibility was "the newly liberated territory or what used to be known as Kotar-Knin." The evidence of Buhin is pertinent. The witness had a sound basis for this evidence, and I refer to transcripts 10049 and 10053. General Ivan Cermak possessed de jure and de facto authority over the units in the Knin garrison area, which comprised the majority of the area of the Split Military District. Article 52 of Exhibit D32, and paragraph 1(e) of Exhibit D33. General Cermak had de facto authority over the units in the larger Split Military District area. Examples of evidence establishing this point, Exhibit D818, the evidence of Flynn, Buhin, Ermolaev. He had the ability to directly investigate and discipline the criminal conduct of the soldiers in these units. He had the ability to initiate investigations into the conduct of the soldiers in these units, using the military police and the civilian police. Contemporaneous documentation prepared by General Cermak confirms that he had command over the troops in the operational zone. On the 11th of August, 1995, General Cermak addressed a letter to General Forand, in relation to the freedom of movement. It's Exhibit P390. In addition to General Forand, Cermak addressed this letter to "the troops in the zone of separation." In his 1998 interview, Cermak explained that this meant the troops in the operational zone. Further, in the 1998 interview, when discussing this letter and incidences where internationals may have experienced problems with freedom of movement, Cermak stated that in these circumstances: "I would immediately phone either the civilian police or the military police, or the operative zones. I would phone them and tell them to tell -- say, tell the units on the ground that people had freedom of movement and to let them through and so on." Extensive evidence from international witnesses confirms that problems with freedom of movement were resolved by General Cermak in precisely the way he describes. Hansen, Hendriks, Liborius. Later, in the year 2001, when General Cermak was again interviewed by the Prosecutor, he realised the implications of this admission and sought to explain this away, stating: "I went a bit too far sending out this letter, but I didn't have the authority to do this." That's the 2001 interview. However, Exhibits D32, D33, P390, and the evidence of the internationals confirms that the statement he made in 1998 is the truth. It is a recurrent theme in the Cermak Defence case. The Trial Chamber is asked to believe that General Cermak kept issuing orders that he didn't have the authority to issue. Further, there is evidence that orders that it is alleged should not have been issued were received and acted on. For example, P509 and P510 and D303, and the evidence that has been given in relation to those documents. The Defence submission is neither compelling on the facts nor an appropriate way to address the test that is applied under Article 7(3). It is an attempt to re-interpret and isolate facts in a technical and nuances way, the way that the law of Article 7(3) does not support and will not bear. The law of Article 7(3) was expressed clearly in the Kordic trial judgement at paragraph 418 where, and I quote: "Whether de jure or de facto, military or civilian, the existence of a position of authority will have to be based upon an assessment of the reality of the authority of the accused." Mr. Kay in his submissions took some time focussing on the use of the words "ordering" and "telling" by the Witness Dzolic, suggesting that the use of these words was of critical significance. However, in a revealing passage at transcript pages 9113 to 9115 the Trial Chamber questioned this witness on this issue, and the reality of the situation was immediately revealed. In answer to the Court's questions the witness stated that he could remember only one instance when General Cermak asked, requested, ordered, or suggested something, and he didn't do it. The reason he didn't is that he couldn't. He didn't have the manpower. That's at transcript 9114, line 12 to 9114 -- 9115, line 4. It is the reality of the authority of General Cermak that is at issue, not the words that any particular witness may use at any particular time. General Cermak cannot hide his authority in semantics. As the Kordic judgement and all of the decisions that have followed it demonstrate, the law will be practical. And the practical reality of the matter is abundantly clear: General Cermak exercised enormous power for many and varied reasons. The international witnesses knew that. The insider witnesses knew that and the contemporaneous records show it. A recording of a conversation between General Cermak and Tudjman in early 1999 reveals General Cermak's true perception of his command authority. Having become aware that he was suspected of war crimes he said to Tudjman: "Norac and Gotovina were conducting military operations. They were in command of the military actions. I was in command of my part and none of us is as bad as to kill." And he also said: "Norac, Gotovina and I, we are all innocent before God. Those are political stories. None of us ordered any killing. That's rubbish." In this conversation, Cermak placed himself together with Norac and Gotovina as a commander, who could issue orders and had responsibility for events in Operation Storm. He observed that he was not an operational commander but he acknowledged that he was in command of his part. Turning now to General Cermak's authority over the military police and the civilian police. Cermak's control over the military police and the civilian police is confirmed by, first, the orders that he issued to them; P512, P513, D303, D503, P509. The fact that he met with them daily. They came to his office every morning and he received reports from them. Witness 84, Witness 86, Buhin, Dzolic, his interview in 1998. The fact that police and military witnesses confirm -- and the third point I'm moving to now, and that is the fact that the police and military witnesses confirm that they were answerable to him. The witness Dzolic, Witness 86, whether they did what he said or they did what he ordered is not irrelevant to the assessment of the factors relating to effective control but the difference in this case is marginal at best and, as demonstrated above, is practically of very little significance. As regards the evidence of the military witness Dzolic, Mr. Kay in his submission indicated that he thought it odd that there could be a dual chain of command. There is nothing odd about that at all. Dzolic acted on orders that were given to him by either Colonel Budimir or General Cermak. It could not be more straightforward. Mr. Kay said that as Defence counsel this paragraph referring to the dual command placed him on "alert." So it should have. In our submission, this evidence at law is sufficient to defeat his 98 bis motion. As regards the civilian police, in his 1998 interview, Cermak gave a clear example demonstrating that he could ensure investigations by the civilian police. He admitted that when televisions he had delivered to a village were looted he "called the civilian police commander" Mr. Gambiroza, and said, Do whatever you want. I want the culprits to be found, and he got everything going. He states that: "Two or three hours went by and the culprits were captured." 1998 interview at page 82. The Defence also raised the so-called UNCRO orders. The principle that is reflected in the order Cermak issued - that's D303 - is clear. Cermak could, if he chose to, if it promoted his objectives, order the civilian and military police to investigate crime. The evidence of the internationals as to General Cermak's authority was also clear. When dealing with the most serious issues humanity can face, issues of life and death, issues of widespread destruction, the decimation of people's lives and communities, they were directed to General Cermak, who told them on a daily basis that he would ensure that these major crimes were investigated and ultimately ensure that these crimes did not continue. The Trial Chamber has seen the television interviews of General Cermak in relation to the events in Grubori, given on the 26th of August, and 27th of August, 1995. P504, P2386. In these interviews General Cermak refers to his personal authority to conduct an investigation or ensure an investigation takes place. He provides a false version of events and he provides false assurances that he would investigate. The Defence submissions concede that General Cermak may have made these representations to the internationals. In his submission, Mr. Kay stated that "even though he may have held himself out or people had expectations of him, the fact of the matter is that that does not determine the matter." The Defence is inviting a conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. President. The Defence is inviting a conclusion that when confronted with these most serious crimes, General Cermak considered it appropriate to pass himself off as someone he wasn't, to mislead UNCIVPOL, ECMM, UNCRO, and the Red Cross. General Cermak didn't mislead the internationals as to who he was; he misled them as to what he knew about the crimes and what he intended to do about them. I would now like to address General Cermak's knowledge and intent. Immediately following his arrival in Knin on the 6th of August, 1995, General Cermak knew that Croatian soldiers were committing crimes. On the 5th of August, 1995, General Forand had already forwarded a request for a meeting. He noted the destruction and looting in this request and said he wasn't satisfied the Croatian army was fully under control. At this early point, he protested the restrictions of freedom of movement and suggested that that will increase suspicions of abuse. That's P347. In terms of notice and knowledge I probably don't have time to go into the details, and I just refer the Court to General Cermak's 1998 interview. He admits he knew about arson, looting. He admits he knew that Kistanje was completely burned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll just cut that short. He was the interface with the internationals. He knew what they knew. He knew what the intelligence services of the Croatian army knew. There's no doubt he knew about crimes, and he also knew that it was the HV committing the crimes. He received the intelligence report that Ms. Gustafson referred to, P918, the one drafted by Tomasovic. It's a familiar document to the Trial Chamber. He admitted in a 7th September 1995 interview in Slobodna Dalmacija that he knew about the looting and torching of homes and that these crimes were most often committed by members of the Croatian army; D59. 2001 interview. In the -- turning now to the issue of killing. In the conversation he had with Tudjman in early 1999, P1144, he said to Tudjman: "You had fighters on the front-line for three, four years. They lost their houses, ancestors' land. They're already a bit damaged by the Vietnam syndrome, and in that state, they were killing." He knew they were killing. He says in his 1998 interview that his first tasks were to urgently start clearing up the area to get rid of the dead bodies. Trial Chamber's received the lists that he had in his possession, that he gave to the internationals. He admits he received the MUP lists in his 2001 interview. Trial Chamber also heard the evidence of the witness Hayden. General Cermak misrepresented the number of civilians killed. First meeting with Hayden, the list that Hayden reviewed showed 41 civilians. General Cermak said there were two. General Cermak also related on the 19th of August, 1995, to Hayden a chilling report. He said when Hayden asked him about summary executions, he said: "There are probably 200 to 300 bodies in the hills with bullet-holes in their heads." That's a General, that is the most powerful person in Knin, that's the person who knew everything that was going on. An unnerving report, and one that at that time is appallingly accurate. I'll move on, Mr. President. I had some more details to address about his failure to act and his awareness and intent that the crimes would be committed. I'll move straight to the Grubori incident. Out of the many hundreds of killing incidents that occurred and the many hundreds of incidents that he knew of, there is only one crime scene that was caught on video by the internationals moments after the commission of the crime. This incident has provided the Trial Chamber with an insight into the way General Cermak denied, covered up, and promoted crime. From the 21st of August, 1995, Cermak was fully informed about the coming special police operations. He met with Markac and Gotovina; Exhibits D561, D562, P1219 and others. General Cermak received maps from General Markac before Markac embarked on operations. General Cermak's 1998 interview. Trial Chamber is familiar with the events in Grubori; I won't detail them again. When the internationals reported the events in Grubori to Cermak's office, Cermak immediately telephoned General Markac. If not immediately, he did it that evening, on the 25th of August, 1995. 2004 Markac interview also confirmed an interview -- interview of General Cermak. He didn't inform the civilian police. He informed his friend and the commander of the units suspected of the crime. First the civilian police knew about it, that was on the 26th at 10.00 a.m., when Romasev reported it to Mihic. Civilian police planned an on-site investigation, Exhibits D57, P503, P501. But parallel with the efforts of the civilian police who were awaiting a meeting on the 27th with General Cermak, parallel with their efforts to ensure an on-site investigation took place, Markac and Cermak were taking steps to ensure that no investigation was conducted. Markac and Sacic were dealing with Celic. Your Honours have heard the evidence and seen Exhibit P563. You've seen the interview that the witness Lyntton conducted with Cermak, where Cermak related a false story. A similarly false story to the one that Sacic was dictating to Celic. Cermak sent Karolj Dondo to the scene. 1645, on the 26th he was in Grubori, telling those that had survived, those that were fortunate enough not to be in the village at the time of the killings and the burning, he was telling them the bodies would be cleaned away. He already knew that there would be no on-site investigation. He recorded that or had it recorded in Exhibit D57, when he returned from the village. It was not until the morning meeting on the 27th of August, 1995, that the chief of the police of the region -- of the Kotar-Knin region and the chief of police of the Knin police station learnt that there would be no investigation. It was only after this meeting that the chief of the Kotar-Knin region recorded in Exhibit P501 that would there would be sanitation of the Grubori village. The investigation recorded and contemplated in that same diary and in other documents was not to take place. Cermak knew the truth on the 25th, when the internationals told his office. He knew the truth when Lyntton told him the truth on the 26th. He knew the truth when he was at the Grubori hamlet. He saw it with his own eyes. He covered it up by denying it. The internationals didn't believe him. But it was his version of events that was the reason there was no investigation into this incident. Mr. President, I see that the clock is running. I will conclude. Through his omissions, Cermak significantly and substantial contributed to the crimes. Had he acted, he would have made the realisation of the crimes that were part of the joint criminal enterprise more difficult. Cermak was the central figure in ensuring that a climate of threat and fear endured and that those Serbs who had not fled the artillery attack would leave the Krajina in fear for their life. Based on his position of authority, Cermak had a duty to protect the Serb population. He failed to so. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I will turn over to Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, unnecessary to remind you that speed of speech is, even if there is only half an hour left, is something to considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will bear that in mind, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will be addressing Court on General Markac's criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) and 7(3). General Markac participated in the joint criminal enterprise. As already referred to, he was present at the 31st July meeting in Brioni and discussed his contribution towards the plan. I'd like to particularly refer Court to page 19 of P461 where General Markac is recorded as stating as follows: "There is no change in the task, except that Mr. Norac is heading upward. That means that we are going to drive them into a pocket here, and from that point we can head towards Norac, while Norac can head towards Lapac, and we have practically evacuated the entire area. Everything fits in and to all practical purposes we gain with this plan proposed by Mr. Gotovina ..." Now this statement resonates with statements made by President Tudjman and General Gotovina, particularly recorded at page 15 of the transcript. General Markac contributed towards the joint criminal enterprise by planning and commanding the special police part of the operation. He was the assistant minister in charge -- assistant minister of interior in charge of the special police sector and its commander. Special police was subordinated to the HV General Staff for Operation Storm, and General Markac was appointed as the action commander. And the chief of General Staff held Mr. Markac personally responsible for the special police part of the operation. I refer to the testimony of witnesses Janic, Turkalj, P554, and D543. General Markac planned the operation in coordination with other members of the JCE. He conducted planning meetings where he briefed his subordinate commanders and provided them with the required intelligence gathered from HV intelligence branches and he also secured the required material. I refer to testimony of Witness Janic, D544 and D545. He issued orders for combat readiness of the units and the special police artillery batteries. I refer to D541, D1206 and D1207. Mr. Russo has already referred to orders issued by General Markac during the course of the operation, so I will not go into that. But I would particularly draw attention of Court to P2385, page 7, and the testimony of witness Janic. After the territory was taken, General Markac also issued orders for mop-up operations which were implemented. P1153, page 6; D562; P574; and P575. He had the material ability to punish his subordinates. The inner control branch of the special police monitored discipline within the special police. The head of inner control department was directly subordinated to the chief of the sector and to General Markac and reported to both. Witness Janic, Turkalj, D528, D529. Witness Turkalj also described the Ministry of Interior disciplinary procedure, in addition to which P2370 extracts of the MUP employment code, Article 49, 59, 60, and P1155, P2364, 2369 - these are all P numbers, Mr. President - 609, 610, 587, reflect General Markac's disciplinary authority over special police units. Witness Janic testified if that a serious crime was committed by a member of the special police, the matter would be reported to the chief of the sector or General Markac who would in turn notify the matter to criminal police for investigation. And independent of that criminal investigation, the special police authorities were required to initiate an internal disciplinary procedure. D530 and D531 reflect General Markac's ability to initiate investigations into crime within the special police itself. Finally, as Witness Janic testified, special police -- members of the special police were policemen themselves, and more importantly, General Markac was an assistant minister of interior and, as such, was well placed to activate the other components of the Ministry of Interior, for example, crime police, if he deemed it necessary. Now, Mr. Russo has already referred to the illegal artillery attack carried out by General Markac. As the special police forces entered the formerly Serb-held territory, they plundered and destroyed civilian property. General Markac ordered or condoned this criminal activity. General Markac commanded and directed the operation in person. He led the troops in person as they advanced. I refer to his 2003 interview, page 53 to 54. The discipline of the special police forces was at a very high level and not a singular part of the special police was out of control. Witness Janic. General Markac entered Gracac at 1001 hours on 5th August, and by 1200, Gracac was completely under the control of the special police. And from that point onwards, the special police headquarters was set up in Gracac and operated there throughout the period relevant to the indictment. Since then there were approximately 500 members of the special police based in Gracac at any given time, and General Markac was present in Gracac fairly regularly. D555, page 29; P238, page 7. Testimony of Janic. Having captured Gracac, General Markac ordered his forces to advance to Donji Lapac. General Markac entered Donji Lapac with his forces around 1.00 or 2.00 p.m. on 7th August and was present in Donji Lapac that night. Janjic, Turkalj, D555, page 47. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence of destruction and of organised looting in Gracac. Witness Steenbergen saw its tensile destruction and looting in Gracac on 6th August. And on 8th August, witness Vanderostyne saw burning buildings in the outskirts of Gracac and photographed special police looting property in the centre of the Gracac town where special police officers were located in the presence of a commander. Witness 82 saw a large amount of houses along the road between Gracac and Donji Lapac burned down or destroyed and members of the special police present in the area while the dwellings were still ablaze. Witness Galbraith saw approximately 70 per cent of the buildings in Donji Lapac systematically torched, and at a meeting on 26 August, minister of defence, Mr. Susak, and the Gospic Military District Commander, Mr. Norac informed President Tudjman that the destruction in Donji Lapac was carried out by General Markac's forces. I refer to P470, page 53 to 54. The burning in Donji Lapac started the very evening special police forces entered the town. General Markac -- and entered the town with General Markac, and everything burned down during that night itself. P586; D556; P470, page 53 to 54. The population in Donji Lapac was 90 to 98 per cent Serb prior to the operation, as already referred to, which reflects the persecutory intent behind the criminal acts. Further, Witness 82 testified to being ordered to mark property with HV or MUP signs which were preserved, while those that were not marked were destroyed. This reflects the systematic nature of the criminal conduct. In addition to the acts of plunder and destruction, the special police killed Serb civilians who remained in the area after the operation. General Markac was aware that killings of Serb civilians was a possible consequence in the execution of the enterprise. He deployed members of the special police who had a propensity for violence and who had been described as undisciplined and nationalistic. Witness Turkalj and P1088, the official note of interview, in fact, reflects the violent disposition of a particular member of the special police regarding whom General Markac was warned prior to the operation. General Markac was thus aware that in a climate where plunder and destruction of property belonging to the Serb population was encouraged Serb civilians could be killed or be subject to inhumane or cruel treatment. General Markac contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by participating in the reporting of false information and thereby encouraged further crimes. The Lucko unit was considered to be an elite unit of the special police and it was deployed in three mop-up operations; one in the area of Petrova Gora on 13th and 14th August; the second in the Plavno valley on 25th August; and the third in the Promina hills on 26th August. Members of the unit committed crimes in two of the three operations which reflects that this was indeed the order of the day. General Markac covered up both crimes. I will refer to the case of Grubori, Mr. President. Due to lack of time, I will not go into the second incident. The crimes committed in the special police operation in Plavno valley have already been addressed at length, so I will only focus on General Markac's personal involvement in the cover-up. Now, conspicuously absent in Mr. Kuzmanovic's address on the incident was a reference to the three reports submitted by General Markac on the incident. In General Markac's first report, on the event of 25th August, that is P575, dated 26 August, General Markac reported that none of the six units which participated in the mop-up operation were involved in combat. Then when he became aware that the incident was receiving scrutiny by the international community, he cancelled P575, and issued P576, also dated 26 August, by which he reported that the Lucko unit had met with resistance and civilians were killed and houses were caught fire in the course of combat. By P576 he also reported that one of the enemy soldiers by the name of Duro Karanovic was killed and another by the name of Stevan Karanovic was arrested. And then in March 1996 when alerted to the fact that this combat version could no longer be sustained in the face of the overwhelming evidence that it was an outright crime, he issued a third report, P505, by which he now reported that the crimes were committed by enemy soldiers. Witness Celic testified regarding General Markac's personal involvement in the cover-up. On 26th August, witness Celic was summoned to General Markac's office where General Markac and Chief of Staff Sacic informed him that an incident had occurred in Grubori, and then he was ordered to write another report. He was not asked questions. He was not asked to provide an explanation as to why he did not report the matter. Instead, he was ordered to write another report. And then soon after that meeting, Celic was taken to another room in the same special police headquarters where Sacic, the Chief of Staff, dictated the new report to him. That is P563. Witness Celic testified that he was completely unaware of the contents of the report and that he merely went along with what he was ordered to do. Court has heard sufficient evidence to conclude that General Markac's reports P576 and P505 are false and that the Lucko unit committed the crime. Members of the unit were present in Grubori at the time. P559, P1226, Celic, Roberts, P28, P561, P562.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you're developing a speed again which is unbearable for all those who are assisting us. Take a breath now and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. May I proceed? None of the units participating in the operation met with any form of resistance contrary to what General Markac reported. Testimony of Janic, Celic, Exhibit P560, P577, page 5, notes of interview of the members of the Lucko unit which have been admitted into evidence. There are several, and I will not go into all of them. And contrary to what is reported in P576, Court has heard testimony that Duro Karanovic was one of the civilians killed in the incident. And P624 and 626 confirm that no one by the name of Stevan Karanovic was ever arrested by Ministry of Interior or, for that matter, Ministry of Defence forces. Similarly, General Markac submitted a false report, P579, in relation to the incidents of burning houses which were -- which was committed by members of the Lucko unit on 26th August in the area of Ramljane. That is in the course of the operation that was conducted on 26th August. Due to lack of time I will not go into details of that incident. General Markac contracted to the joint criminal enterprise by his failure to act, namely, his failure to investigate and punish subordinates for crimes committed, thereby he encouraged the commission of further crimes. By his failure to act, General Markac sent out a message to his subordinates that crimes could be committed with impunity. In fact the statement made by member of the special police soon after he burned houses in Ramljane to General Markac to the effect, So I did it, so I burnt them, so what now? Kill me if you want, captures the sense of the command climate he created which encouraged his subordinates to commit crimes. I will now address Court on General Markac's 7(3) liability, his command responsibility. The evidence that I've already discussed establishes that he had effective control over his subordinates and that he had notice of crimes, particularly Grubori, the destruction in Gracac, Donji Lapac, and Ramljane. In addition, General Markac admitted in statement that he had indeed seen destruction. This is at page 44 of his 2004 statement. He says: "Look, I don't know that they were deliberately burned. I saw there houses that were burned but I can't say it was deliberate, and I can't whether it was during Operation Storm or after." Further, the number of burials in the cemetery in Gracac, which were increasing by the day, placed him on inquiry notice of the killings. I refer to P41, P49, P35. And he knew of crimes committed in previous operations. I refer to his 2002 statement, page 59 to 61, 81 to 82, 88 to 89. Notwithstanding General Markac's knowledge of -- knowledge that his subordinates had committed crimes, he failed to take reasonable measures to prevent crimes by his subordinates. He failed to issue a specific order prohibiting crimes prior to the operation and in the face of extensive crimes committed in the course of the operation, for instance, in the case of Grubori and Ramljane he still did not issue a single order to prevent further crimes. I draw Court's attention to P556 and P557. He deployed members of the special police who had a propensity for violence, notwithstanding warnings from his subordinated commanders. By failing to act, on receipt of notice of crimes, he failed to prevent further crimes. For example, he received notice of crimes committed in Grubori on 25th August itself. And he was aware that the same units were to be deployed the next day in the course of an operation. Yet his failure to withdraw the units immediately, at least on the 25th evening or 26th morning prior to the next day's operation, led to the crimes committed by the same unit on the 26th. He failed to prevent the crimes on 26th by his failure to act on 25th, regarding the crimes committed in Grubori. General Markac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish crimes by his subordinates. Witnesses Janic and Turkalj testified that no member of the special police was investigated and punished for crimes committed during or in the aftermath of Operation Storm. The Grubori incident was not investigated by any authority, either the special police or the civilian police, until witness Zganjer, the Sibenik prosecutor, initiated an investigation in 2001. Instead of punishment, all members of the special police who participated in Operation Storm, including those who committed crimes, were awarded medals. Particularly the member of the special police who admitted to General Markac that he burned houses on 26th August, Franjo Drljo was promoted. I refer to testimony of witness Celic, P1237, page 4; and P616. In addition to the modes of liability that are covered, Mr. President, Your Honours, if the Trial Chamber does not find General Markac to have participated in a joint criminal enterprise, the evidence referred to allows the Chamber to find him criminally responsible under Article 7(1) for ordering or aiding and abetting the crimes charged in the indictment. In conclusion, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that it has adduced sufficient evidence upon which the Trial Chamber could convict Generals Ante Gotovina, Ivan Cermak, and Mladen Markac as charged in the indictment. This concludes the Prosecution addresses.
